class/Backpack.d:
Tool objects in the Backpack container make up the player's inventory and display as icon buttons at the bottom of the screen. See in‑game tools for more information.

When a player's character spawns, the contents of StarterPack and the player's StarterGear clone to Backpack. When the character dies, the client destroys the Backpack and replaces it with a new one, populated again with the contents of StarterPack and StarterGear.

To disable the default Roblox inventory GUI and replace it with your own, call StarterGui:SetCoreGuiEnabled() in a LocalScript as outlined in disable default UI.

Backpack can be accessed from both the client and the server:
class/Backpack.s: A container object that holds a player's inventory. Any `Class.Tool` in a player's `Backpack` will be displayed in their inventory at the bottom of the screen.

kid.simple: The Backpack is the player's inventory. It's a folder inside each Player, and every Tool in it shows up as a button on the hotbar at the bottom of the screen. When the player picks a tool to hold, the tool leaves the Backpack and goes into their character's hand.
kid.analogy: The Backpack is like a school bag. Your tools wait in it until you pull one out to use. But this bag is magic: every time you respawn you get a brand-new bag, refilled from StarterPack and your StarterGear.
whenToUse: Give a player a tool for this life: clone it into player.Backpack.
Check what tools a player has.
Take tools away from a player.
kid.where: Inside every Player: `player.Backpack` or `player:WaitForChild("Backpack")`. Both the server and the player's own device can see it. A LocalScript can get its own with `Players.LocalPlayer:WaitForChild("Backpack")`.

terms.Tool: An item a player can hold and use, like a sword.
terms.inventory: The list of items a player is carrying.
terms.StarterPack: A service in Studio. Its tools are copied into every player's Backpack each time they spawn.
terms.StarterGear: A folder inside each Player. Its tools are copied into that one player's Backpack each time they spawn.
terms.equip: Take a tool out of the Backpack to hold it. While held it lives in the character Model, not the Backpack.
terms.spawn: When a character appears in the world (first time or after dying).
terms.clone: Make a copy of an object with :Clone().

examples.title: Give a tool, and give it back after every respawn
examples.place: Script in ServerScriptService (put a Tool named Flashlight in ServerStorage)
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local ServerStorage = game:GetService("ServerStorage")
local flashlight = ServerStorage:WaitForChild("Flashlight")

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    player.CharacterAdded:Connect(function()
        -- A new Backpack is made every spawn, so give the tool every spawn
        local backpack = player:WaitForChild("Backpack")
        flashlight:Clone().Parent = backpack
    end)
end)
explain: When a character spawns, Roblox makes a fresh Backpack and fills it from StarterPack and the player's StarterGear.
When the character dies, the old Backpack (and anything you put in it) is thrown away.
So we clone the flashlight into the Backpack inside CharacterAdded, which runs after every spawn.
An easier way for one player: put the tool in player.StarterGear once and Roblox does this for you.

examples.title: List all tools a player has (held or not)
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

local function listTools(player)
    local names = {}
    -- Tools waiting in the Backpack
    for _, item in player.Backpack:GetChildren() do
        if item:IsA("Tool") then
            table.insert(names, item.Name)
        end
    end
    -- The tool currently held is inside the character, not the Backpack
    local character = player.Character
    if character then
        local held = character:FindFirstChildOfClass("Tool")
        if held then
            table.insert(names, held.Name .. " (held)")
        end
    end
    return names
end

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    player.CharacterAdded:Connect(function()
        task.wait(1)
        print(player.Name .. " has: " .. table.concat(listTools(player), ", "))
    end)
end)
explain: Backpack:GetChildren() lists tools that are NOT being held.
The held tool is inside the character Model, so we check there too.
table.concat joins the names into one line of text.

gotchas: Tools placed only in the Backpack disappear when the player dies, because the Backpack is replaced.
A held tool is in player.Character, not in the Backpack.
To hide the default hotbar and make your own, call StarterGui:SetCoreGuiEnabled(Enum.CoreGuiType.Backpack, false) in a LocalScript.

class/BadgeService.d: BadgeService provides information and functionality related to badges. Badges are used across the platform to recognize a player's achievements and activity. Upon awarding a badge to a player, it is added to their inventory and displayed on their profile page.
class/BadgeService.s: Provides information on badges and awards them.

m.d:
Grants a Player a badge with the UserId and the badge ID.

In order to successfully award a badge:

  • The player must be presently connected to the experience.
  • The player must not already have the badge (note that a player may delete an awarded badge from their profile and be awarded the badge again).
  • The badge must be awarded from a server script (a Script with RunContext of RunContext.Server or RunContext.Legacy) or a ModuleScript eventually required by one, not from a client script.
  • The badge must be awarded in a place that is part of the experience associated with the badge.
  • The badge must be enabled; check this using the IsEnabled property of the badge fetched through BadgeService:GetBadgeInfoAsync().

Rate limit is 50 + 35 * [number of users] per minute.

m.d:
Checks a list of badge IDs against a UserId and returns a list of badge IDs that the player owns. This method supports batches of up to 10 badges; use BadgeService:UserHasBadgeAsync() for single badge lookups.

When called from a server script, any UserId can be used. If the user with the target user ID has not recently been in the server, only badge IDs that are associated with the requesting experience will be checked, and any badge IDs that are not associated with the requesting experience will not be included in the response (as if they were not owned).

For users that have recently been in the server, any badges for any experiences can be queried, no matter who created the badge or which experience it is used for.

In a client script (a LocalScript or a Script with RunContext of RunContext.Client), only the UserId of the local user whose client is running the script can be used.

Rate limit is 10 + 5 * [number of players] per minute in each server.

Checks a list of badge IDs against a User and returns, for each badge the player owns, a dictionary containing the badge's ID and the date it was awarded. This method supports batches of up to 100 badges; use BadgeService:UserHasBadgeAsync() for single badge lookups.

Each entry in the returned list is a dictionary with the following fields:

Key Type Description
BadgeId int64 The ID of the owned badge.

When called from a server script, any User can be used. If the user with the target User has not recently been in the server, only badge IDs that are associated with the requesting experience will be checked, and any badge IDs that are not associated with the requesting experience will not be included in the response (as if they were not owned).

For users that have recently been in the server, any badges for any experiences can be queried, no matter who created the badge or which experience it is used for.

In a client script (a LocalScript or a Script with RunContext of RunContext.Client), only the User of the local user whose client is running the script can be used.

Rate limit is 10 + 5 * [number of players] per minute in each server.

Empty if none of the provided badges are owned by the given user. Not guaranteed to be in the same order as the input list. Some badge IDs may be omitted if the user with the target User has not recently been in the server and the badge IDs are not associated with the requesting experience.

m.d:
This function returns whether the badge with the given ID is marked disabled on the Roblox website. A badge can be disabled by its owner on its page on the Roblox website, in the settings sub-menu. When a badge is disabled, this function returns true and the badge can no longer be awarded. A badge may be quickly re-enabled through the same menu.

In Studio, a badge can only be tested if it is disabled. Calling this function with an enabled badge in Studio will return true and produce a warning "Sorry, badges can only be tested if they are disabled on Roblox game servers".

Note that even if a badge is enabled it may not necessarily be awardable (for example if it isn't associated with the current game).

Badges that are associated with special events are a common reason for a badge to be disabled. Often, it is easier to simply disable a badge instead of hard-coding a time check for when some event ends.
m.s: Returns whether a given badge is disabled.

p.s: The ID of the badge.

r.s: True if the specified badge is not available to be awarded.

m.dep: This function is deprecated. Do not use it for new work. Instead, it can be checked by calling BadgeService:GetBadgeInfoAsync() and checking the IsEnabled field.

m.d:

Badges can only be awarded from a place that is part of the game associated with the badge. This means, for example, a developer cannot award a badge associated with another developer's game.

Even if this returns true, a badge may still not be award-able. For example, it may be disabled.
m.s: Determines if a given badge is associated with the current game.

class/BallSocketConstraint.d:
A BallSocketConstraint constrains its Attachments so that they occupy the same position. By default it allows both attachments to freely rotate about all of their axes, but if LimitsEnabled is true, the attachments can only rotate in a limited cone.

Note that if this constraint attaches one part (A) to another part (B) that is anchored or connected to an anchored part (Z), part A will not be locally simulated when interacting with a player.

When configuring this constraint, it may be helpful to study Roblox Units to understand how Roblox units compare to metric units.

Limits

You can set limits to restrict both tilt and twist of a ball socket, similar to how a human's head can tilt and turn within a limited axial range. Enabling the LimitsEnabled property exposes the UpperAngle value to restrict tilt within a cone; it also exposes the TwistLimitsEnabled property which, when enabled, lets you restrict twist rotation through the TwistLowerAngle and TwistUpperAngle limits.
class/BallSocketConstraint.s: Forces its two attachments into the same position and allows them to freely rotate about all three axes, with optional limits to restrict both tilt and twist.

m.d: Sets whether the BallSocketConstraint has a limit on rotation based on UpperAngle. When true, it enforces that its Attachment1 isn't rotated more than a set angle from its Attachment0.
m.s: Sets whether the `BallSocketConstraint` sets a limit on rotation based on `Class.BallSocketConstraint.UpperAngle|UpperAngle`.

kid.simple: If true, Attachment1 cannot tilt more than UpperAngle away from Attachment0. Also unlocks the twist limit settings.
kid.example: workspace.Lamp.BallSocketConstraint.LimitsEnabled = true

m.d:
Sets the maximum frictional torque applied to keep its Attachments aligned.

MaxFrictionTorque specifies the stiffness of the BallSocketConstraint (how much it resists rotation around its Attachments).
m.s: Sets the maximum frictional torque applied to keep its `Class.Attachment|Attachments` aligned.

kid.simple: How stiff the joint is: the most twisting friction it uses to resist turning. 0 = totally floppy; higher = stiffer.
kid.example: workspace.Ragdoll.Neck.MaxFrictionTorque = 20

kid.example: workspace.Lamp.BallSocketConstraint.Radius = 0.3

m.d: How elastic Attachments connected by a BallSocketConstraint will be when they reach the end of the range specified by UpperAngle when LimitsEnabled is true. Constrained between 0 and 1.
m.s: How elastic `Class.Attachment|Attachments` connected by a `BallSocketConstraint` will be when they reach the end of the range specified by `Class.BallSocketConstraint.UpperAngle|UpperAngle` when `Class.BallSocketConstraint.LimitsEnabled|LimitsEnabled` is `true`.

kid.simple: How bouncy the joint is when it hits the UpperAngle limit, from 0 (no bounce) to 1 (full bounce). Needs LimitsEnabled.

m.d: Sets whether the BallSocketConstraint sets a limit on twist rotation based on TwistUpperAngle and TwistLowerAngle. The twist angle is defined as the angle between the Y axis of Attachment1 and the Y axis of Attachment0.
m.s: Sets whether the `BallSocketConstraint` sets a limit on twist rotation based on `Class.BallSocketConstraint.TwistUpperAngle|TwistUpperAngle` and `Class.BallSocketConstraint.TwistLowerAngle|TwistLowerAngle`.

kid.simple: BallSocketConstraint pins two attachments to the same spot but lets them turn in any direction. With limits on, you can stop it tilting too far (a cone limit) and stop it twisting too much (twist limits).
kid.analogy: BallSocketConstraint is like your shoulder or hip joint: the arm stays attached at one point but can swing around in almost any direction. Limits are like how your neck can only turn and tilt so far.

kid.where: Make it with Instance.new("BallSocketConstraint"), set Attachment0 and Attachment1 (one in each part, placed where the joint should be) and put it in workspace.

terms.constraint: An invisible rule or connector that the physics engine follows, like 'these two parts must stay stuck together' or 'push this part upward'.
terms.attachment: A tiny invisible point you put inside a part. It has a position AND a direction (its own X, Y and Z arrows). Constraints grab parts by their attachments.
terms.Attachment0 / Attachment1: The two attachments a constraint connects. Attachment0 is usually the one that gets pushed or moved; Attachment1 is the other end or the goal.
terms.torque: A twisting push that makes things spin, like turning a doorknob or a steering wheel. Torque = force x distance from the spinning point, so pushing farther from the center twists harder.
terms.anchored: An anchored part is frozen in place. Physics and constraint forces cannot move it. Set `part.Anchored = false` if you want a constraint to move it.
terms.unanchored: A part that physics is allowed to move. Constraints that push or pull only work on unanchored parts.
terms.restitution: Bounciness, from 0 (no bounce, just stops) to 1 (bounces back as hard as it hit).
terms.limits: Stops that keep a joint from moving too far, like a door that can only swing 90 degrees.
terms.stiffness: How strong a spring is. A stiff spring pushes back hard when you squash or stretch it even a little.
terms.tilt: Leaning to the side away from straight, like nodding or tipping your head.
terms.twist: Turning around the joint's own line, like shaking your head 'no'. It is measured between the two attachments' Y arrows.
terms.friction torque: A twisting resistance that makes the joint stiff, so it does not flop around freely.
terms.degrees: The usual way to measure angles: 90 degrees is a quarter turn.

examples.title: A floppy hanging lamp
examples.code:
local ceiling = workspace:WaitForChild("Ceiling") -- anchored
local lamp = workspace:WaitForChild("Lamp")       -- unanchored, hanging below

-- The joint point: the top of the lamp
local jointSpot = lamp.CFrame * CFrame.new(0, lamp.Size.Y / 2, 0)

local a0 = Instance.new("Attachment")
a0.Parent = ceiling
a0.WorldCFrame = jointSpot
local a1 = Instance.new("Attachment")
a1.Parent = lamp
a1.WorldCFrame = jointSpot

local socket = Instance.new("BallSocketConstraint")
socket.Attachment0 = a0
socket.Attachment1 = a1
socket.LimitsEnabled = true
socket.UpperAngle = 30          -- can tilt at most 30 degrees
socket.MaxFrictionTorque = 50   -- a little stiffness so it does not swing forever
socket.Parent = ceiling
explain: Both attachments go at the top of the lamp, so that is the pivot point.
LimitsEnabled with UpperAngle 30 means the lamp can tilt up to 30 degrees in any direction, but not more.
MaxFrictionTorque adds stiffness so bumps die down instead of swinging forever.

gotchas: Put both attachments at the exact same spot (the joint), or the parts will jump together when the game starts.
UpperAngle only works when LimitsEnabled is true; twist limits also need TwistLimitsEnabled.

If a part is joined this way to an anchored part (or something connected to an anchored part), its physics is not calculated on the player's own device when they touch it, so it may feel slightly delayed.

class/BanHistoryPages.d:
BanHistoryPages is returned by Players:GetBanHistoryAsync(). This instance allows an experience to view the entire ban and unban history of any player within the experience's universe.

The items within BanHistoryPages are tables with the following fields:

Name Type Description
DisplayReason string The DisplayReason that was shown to the user
PrivateReason string The PrivateReason that was sent with this ban.
StartTime string The time that this ban was applied in ISO 8601 format.
Duration number The length of the ban in seconds. If it is a permanent ban, it will be -1.
Ban boolean If the action was a ban, it will be true. If the action was an unban, it will be false.
PlaceId number The place in which a ban or unban was explicitly updated. This field is -1 if the action was applied on the universe level.
class/BanHistoryPages.s: Returned by `Class.Players:GetBanHistoryAsync` to view the entire ban and unban history of any UserId.

class/BaseCoreGuiConfiguration.d:
BaseCoreGuiConfiguration is the base class inherited by the per-element configuration objects that control Roblox's built-in CoreGui elements: PlayerListConfiguration, SelfViewConfiguration, and CapturesViewConfiguration. Each of these concrete configuration objects is created automatically as a child of the CoreGuiConfiguration service.

It defines the shared Enabled property that toggles whether the corresponding core GUI element is enabled.
class/BaseCoreGuiConfiguration.s: Base class for the configuration objects that control individual built-in `Class.CoreGui` elements.

m.d:
When true, the built-in CoreGui element associated with the inheriting configuration object is enabled; when false, that element is disabled. Enabled is not the same as currently shown. Defaults to true.

Each concrete subclass — PlayerListConfiguration, SelfViewConfiguration, and CapturesViewConfiguration — inherits this property to toggle its respective element.
m.s: Determines whether the built-in `Class.CoreGui` element controlled by this configuration object is enabled.

class/BasePart.d:
BasePart is an abstract base class for in-world objects that render and are physically simulated while in the Workspace. There are several implementations of BasePart, the most common being Part and MeshPart. Others include WedgePart, SpawnLocation, and the singleton Terrain object. Generally, when documentation refers to a "part," most BasePart implementations will work and not just Part.

For information on how BaseParts are grouped into simulated rigid bodies, see Assemblies.

There are many different objects that interact with BasePart (other than Terrain), including:

  • Several BaseParts may be grouped within a Model and moved at the same time using PVInstance:PivotTo(). See Models.
  • A Decal applies a stretched image texture to the faces of a BasePart, while a Texture applies a tiled image texture to the faces. See Textures and Decals.
  • A SurfaceGui renders GuiObjects on the face of a part. See In-Experience UI Containers.
  • Attachments can be added to a BasePart to specify CFrames relative to the part. These are often used by physical Constraint objects as outlined in Mechanical Constraints and Mover Constraints.
  • ParticleEmitter objects emit particles uniformly in the volume of the BasePart to which they are parented. See Particle Emitters.
  • Light objects like PointLight emit light from the center of a BasePart as illustrated in Light Sources.
  • If parented to a Tool and given the name Handle, a BasePart can be held by characters. See In-Experience Tools.
class/BasePart.s: The abstract base class for in-world objects that physically interact.

m.d:
The Anchored property determines whether the part will be immovable by physics. When enabled, a part will never change position due to gravity, other part collisions, overlapping other parts, or any other physics-related causes. As a result, two anchored parts will never fire the Touched event on each other.

An anchored part may still be moved by changing its CFrame or Position, and it still may have a nonzero AssemblyLinearVelocity and AssemblyAngularVelocity.

Finally, if an unanchored part is joined with an anchored part through an object like a Weld, it too will act anchored. If such a joint breaks, the part may be affected by physics again. See Assemblies for more details.

Network ownership cannot be set on anchored parts. If a part's anchored status changes on the server, the network ownership of that part will be affected.
m.s: Determines whether a part is immovable by physics.

kid.simple: If true, the part is frozen in place: gravity, bumps, and pushes cannot move it. Scripts can still move it by setting Position or CFrame. Use it for floors, walls, and anything that should not fall.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Anchored = true -- stays floating in the air
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 20, 0)
part.Parent = Workspace
kid.gotcha: An unanchored part welded to an anchored part acts anchored too.

m.d:
The angular velocity vector of this part's assembly. It's the rate of change of orientation in radians per second.

Angular velocity is the same at every point of the assembly.

Setting the velocity directly may lead to unrealistic motion. Using Torque or AngularVelocity constraint is preferred, or use ApplyAngularImpulse() if you want instantaneous change in velocity.

If the part is owned by the server, this property must be changed from a server Script (not from a LocalScript or a Script with RunContext set to RunContext.Client). If the part is owned by a client through automatic ownership, this property can be changed from either a client script or a server script; changing it from a client script for a server-owned part will have no effect.
m.s: The angular velocity of the part's assembly.

kid.simple: How fast the part's assembly (it and everything welded to it) is spinning, and around which axis, in radians per second. You can set it, but a Torque or AngularVelocity constraint gives smoother results.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
part.Anchored = false
-- spin around the up (Y) axis at about one full turn per second
part.AssemblyAngularVelocity = Vector3.new(0, 2 * math.pi, 0)

m.d:
A position calculated via the Mass and Position of all the parts in the assembly.

If the assembly has an anchored part, that part's center of mass will be the assembly's center of mass, and the assembly will have infinite mass.

Knowing the center of mass can help the assembly maintain stability. A force applied to the center of mass will not cause angular acceleration, only linear. An assembly with a low center of mass will have a better time staying upright under the effect of gravity.
m.s: The center of mass of the part's assembly in world space.

kid.simple: Read-only. The balance point of the whole assembly, as a position in the world. If the assembly has an anchored part, that part's center is used.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
print(part.AssemblyCenterOfMass)

m.d:
The linear velocity vector of this part's assembly. It's the rate of change in position of AssemblyCenterOfMass in studs per second.

If you want to know the velocity at a point other than the assembly's center of mass, use GetVelocityAtPosition().

Setting the velocity directly may lead to unrealistic motion. Using a VectorForce constraint is preferred, or use ApplyImpulse() if you want instantaneous change in velocity.

If the part is owned by the server, this property must be changed from a server Script (not from a LocalScript or a Script with RunContext set to RunContext.Client). If the part is owned by a client through automatic ownership, this property can be changed from either a client script or a server script; changing it from a client script for a server-owned part will have no effect.
m.s: The linear velocity of the part's assembly.

kid.simple: How fast and in which direction the assembly is moving, in studs per second. Setting it makes the part suddenly move at that speed, which is handy for launch pads.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
part.Anchored = false
-- move 30 studs per second along X and 50 per second upward
part.AssemblyLinearVelocity = Vector3.new(30, 50, 0)
kid.gotcha: For forces that last, use a constraint like LinearVelocity; for a single shove, `ApplyImpulse` respects weight better.

m.d:
The sum of the mass of all the BaseParts in this part's assembly. Parts that are Massless and are not the assembly's root part will not contribute to the AssemblyMass.

If the assembly has an anchored part, the assembly's mass is considered infinite. Constraints and other physical interactions between unanchored assemblies with a large difference in mass may cause instabilities.
m.s: The total mass of the part's assembly.

kid.simple: Read-only. The total weight of all the parts in this assembly. If any part in it is anchored, the mass counts as infinite.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
print("Total mass:", part.AssemblyMass)

m.d:
This property indicates the BasePart automatically chosen to represent the assembly's root part. If the part is not parented to the Workspace, this property will be nil.

The root part can be changed by changing the RootPriority of the parts in the assembly.

Parts that all share the same AssemblyRootPart are in the same assembly.

For more information on root parts, see Assemblies.
m.s: A reference to the root part of the assembly.

kid.simple: Read-only. The part chosen as the main part of this assembly. Parts that share the same root part are in the same assembly. It is nil if the part is not in Workspace.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
print(part.AssemblyRootPart.Name)

m.d:
AudioCanCollide determines whether the part will physically interact with audio simulation, similar to CastShadow for lighting.

When disabled, audio passes through the part; it is not occluded or reflected.
m.s: Determines whether the part will physically interact with audio simulation, similar to `Class.BasePart.CastShadow|CastShadow` for lighting.

kid.simple: If true, the part blocks and bounces sound in the audio system, a bit like how CastShadow blocks light. If false, sound passes right through it.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
part.AudioCanCollide = false -- sound goes through this curtain

Other visual properties of a part are determined by Transparency and Reflectance.
m.s: Determines the color of a part.

local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

m.d:
CanCollide determines whether a part will physically interact with other parts. When disabled, other parts can pass through the part uninterrupted. Parts used for decoration usually have CanCollide disabled, as they need not be considered by the physics engine.

If a part is not Anchored and has CanCollide disabled, it may fall out of the world to be eventually destroyed by Workspace.FallenPartsDestroyHeight.

When CanCollide is disabled, parts may still fire the Touched event (as well the other parts touching them). You can disable this with CanTouch.

For more information on collisions, see Collisions.
m.s: Determines whether a part may collide with other parts.

kid.simple: If true, other parts and players bump into this part. If false, they walk right through it, like a ghost wall or a decoration.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
part.CanCollide = false
part.Transparency = 0.5 -- see-through ghost wall
kid.gotcha: An unanchored part with CanCollide false will fall through the floor and out of the world.

m.d:
This property determines whether the part is considered during spatial query operations, such as GetPartBoundsInBox or Raycast. Note that CanCollide must be disabled for CanQuery to take effect, and spatial query functions will never include parts with CanQuery of false.

Beyond this property, it is also possible to exclude parts which are descendants of a given list of parts using an OverlapParams or RaycastParams object when calling the spatial query functions.
m.s: Determines whether the part is considered during spatial query operations.

kid.simple: If false, searches like raycasts and "what parts are in this box" skip this part. It only matters when CanCollide is false (colliding parts are always found).
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
part.CanCollide = false
part.CanQuery = false -- raycasts ignore this invisible trigger zone

m.d:
This property determines if Touched and TouchEnded events fire on the part. If true, other touching parts must also have CanTouch set to true for touch events to fire. If false, touch events cannot be set up for the part and attempting to do so will throw an error. Similarly, if the property is set to false after a touch event is connected, the event will be disconnected and the TouchTransmitter removed.

Note that this collision logic can be set to respect collision groups through the Workspace.TouchesUseCollisionGroups property. If true, parts in non-colliding groups will ignore both collisions and touch events, thereby making this property irrelevant.

Performance

There is a small performance gain on parts that have both CanTouch and CanCollide set to false, as these parts will never need to compute any kind of part to part collisions. However, they can still be hit by Raycasts and OverlapParams queries.
m.s: Determines if `Class.BasePart.Touched|Touched` and `Class.BasePart.TouchEnded|TouchEnded` events fire on the part.

kid.simple: If false, the Touched and TouchEnded events do not fire for this part. Both parts must have CanTouch on for a touch to count.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
part.CanTouch = false -- this part ignores touches

m.d:
Determines whether or not a part casts a shadow. Disabling this property for a given part can cause visual artifacts on the shadows cast upon that part.

This property is not designed for performance enhancement, but in complex scenes, strategically disabling it on certain parts can improve performance. Due to the possibility of visual artifacts, we recommend leaving it enabled on all parts in most situations.
m.s: Determines whether or not a part casts a shadow.

kid.simple: If true (the default), the part makes a shadow. Turning it off can help speed in huge scenes but can look odd, so usually leave it on.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
part.CastShadow = false

m.d: The CenterOfMass property describes the local position of a part's center of mass. If this is a single part assembly, this is the AssemblyCenterOfMass converted from world space to local. On simple Parts, the center of mass is always (0, 0, 0), but it can vary for WedgePart or MeshPart.
m.s: Describes the local position of a part's center of mass, relative to its `Class.BasePart.CFrame|CFrame`.

kid.simple: Read-only. The part's balance point measured from the part's own center (local space). For a simple block it is (0, 0, 0), the exact center; a wedge's balance point is off-center.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
print(part.CenterOfMass) --> 0, 0, 0 for a block

m.d:
The CFrame property determines both the position and orientation of the BasePart in the world. It acts as an arbitrary reference location on the geometry, but ExtentsCFrame represents the actual CFrame of its physical center.

When setting CFrame on a part, other joined parts are also moved relative to the part, but it is recommended that you use PVInstance:PivotTo() to move an entire model, such as when teleporting a player's character.

Unlike setting BasePart.Position, setting CFrame will always move the part to the exact given CFrame; in other words: no overlap checking is done and the physics solver will attempt to resolve any overlap unless both parts are Anchored.

For keeping track of positions relative to a part's CFrame, an Attachment may be useful.
m.s: Determines the position and orientation of the `Class.BasePart` in the world.

kid.simple: The part's position AND rotation together in one value. Setting it moves and turns the part in one step, to exactly the spot you say. Multiplying by another CFrame moves the part relative to the way it is facing.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
-- Place at (0, 10, 0), tilted 45 degrees around X
part.CFrame = CFrame.new(0, 10, 0) * CFrame.Angles(math.rad(45), 0, 0)
-- Move 3 studs UP from the part's own point of view (local space)
part.CFrame = part.CFrame * CFrame.new(0, 3, 0)
kid.gotcha: Setting CFrame does not check for overlap; the part goes exactly there even if it is inside another part. To move a model, use `PivotTo`.

m.d:
The CollisionGroup property describes the name of the part's collision group (maximum of 100 characters). Parts start off in the default group whose name is "Default". This value cannot be empty.

Although this property itself is non-replicated, the engine internally replicates the value through another private property to solve backward compatibility issues.
m.s: Describes the name of a part's collision group.

kid.simple: The name of the collision group this part belongs to ("Default" at first). With PhysicsService you can make some groups not bump into others, like letting players walk through team doors.
kid.example:
local PhysicsService = game:GetService("PhysicsService")
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
PhysicsService:RegisterCollisionGroup("Ghosts")
PhysicsService:CollisionGroupSetCollidable("Ghosts", "Ghosts", false)
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
part.CollisionGroup = "Ghosts"

m.d:
The BasePart.CollisionGroupId property describes the ID number of the part's collision group. Parts start off in the "Default" group whose ID is 0. If a part is unregistered, the value becomes -1. This value cannot be less than -1 and it cannot exceed WorldRoot:GetMaxCollisionGroups(). Invalid IDs are clamped.

Although this property can be directly changed, it's recommended that you specify the collision group by setting BasePart.CollisionGroup to the collision group's name.
m.s: Describes the automatically set ID number of a part's collision group.
m.dep: Deprecated.

kid.simple: Old — use `CollisionGroup` instead.

The Color property determines the color of a part. If the part has a Material, this also determines the color used when rendering the material texture.

If this property is set, BrickColor will use the closest match to this Color value.

Other visual properties of a part are determined by Transparency and Reflectance.
m.s: Determines the color of a part.

kid.simple: The part's exact color as a Color3 (red, green, blue). Use `Color3.fromRGB` with numbers from 0 to 255.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
part.Color = Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 255) -- bright pink

m.d:
CurrentPhysicalProperties indicates the current physical properties of the part. You can set custom values for the physical properties per part, custom material, and material override. The Roblox engine prioritizes more granular definitions when determining the effective physical properties of a part. The values in the following list are in order from highest to lowest priority:

  • Custom physical properties of the part
  • Custom physical properties of the part's custom material
  • Custom physical properties of the material override of the part's material
  • Default physical properties of the part's material
m.s: Indicates the current physical properties of the part.

kid.simple: Read-only. The physical settings (density, friction, bounciness) the part is actually using right now, after checking its custom settings and material.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
print(part.CurrentPhysicalProperties.Friction)

m.d:
CustomPhysicalProperties lets you customize various physical aspects of a part, such as its density, friction, and elasticity.

If enabled, this property let's you configure these physical properties. If disabled, these physical properties are determined by the Material of the part.
m.s: Determines several physical properties of a part.

kid.simple: Lets you set your own density (how heavy for its size), friction (how grippy), and elasticity (how bouncy) instead of using the material's normal values. Set it to nil to go back to the material's values.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
-- density 0.7, friction 0.3, elasticity 1 (super bouncy)
part.CustomPhysicalProperties = PhysicalProperties.new(0.7, 0.3, 1)

m.d: The Elasticity of a part is now determined by either its Material or its CustomPhysicalProperties.
m.s: Used to control the Elasticity of the part, but it no longer does anything.
m.dep: This is only one of multiple physics-related properties. It has been deprecated in favor of BasePart.CustomPhysicalProperties, which combines these properties into one.

m.d: When true, and when Workspace.FluidForces is enabled, causes the physics engine to compute aerodynamic forces on this BasePart.

kid.simple: If true, and the experimental `Workspace.FluidForces` setting is on, air pushes on this part, like wind on a paper plane.
kid.example:

local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
part.EnableFluidForces = true

m.d: The CFrame of the physical extents of the BasePart, representing its physical center.

kid.simple: Read-only. The CFrame of the part's real physical center. For most simple parts it matches CFrame, but for some meshes the CFrame point is not the true middle.

m.d: The actual physical size of the BasePart as regarded by the physics engine, for example in collision detection.
m.s: The actual physical size of the `Class.BasePart` as regarded by the physics engine.

local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
print(part.ExtentsSize)

m.d:
The LocalTransparencyModifier property is a multiplier to Transparency that is only visible to the local client. It does not replicate from client to server and is useful for when a part should not render for a specific client, such as how the player does not see their character's body parts when they zoom into first person mode.

This property modifies the local part's transparency through the following formula, with resulting values clamped between 0 and 1.

1 - ((1 - Transparency) × (1 - LocalTransparencyModifier))

Class.BasePart.Transparency|Transparency LocalTransparencyModifier Server-Side Client-Side
0.5 0 0.5 0.5
0.5 0.25 0.5 0.625
0.5 0.5 0.5 0.75
0.5 0.75 0.5 0.875
0.5 1 0.5 1
m.s: Determines a multiplier for `Class.BasePart.Transparency` that is only visible to the local client.

kid.simple: Extra see-through-ness that only the local player sees. Roblox uses it to hide your own body when you zoom into first person. Changes are not shared with the server or other players.
kid.example:
-- LocalScript in StarterCharacterScripts
local character = script.Parent
local head = character:WaitForChild("Head")
head.LocalTransparencyModifier = 1 -- only YOU stop seeing your head

m.d: The Locked property determines whether a part (or a Model it is contained within) may be selected in Studio by clicking on it. This property is most often enabled on parts within environment models that aren't being edited at the moment.
m.s: Determines whether a part is selectable in Studio.

kid.simple: If true, you cannot select the part by clicking it in Studio. Great for stopping yourself from accidentally moving the map while building. It does nothing during play.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
part.Locked = true

m.d:
Mass is a read-only property that describes the product of a part's volume and density. It is returned by the GetMass() function.

  • The volume of a part is determined by its Size and its Shape, which varies depending on the kind of BasePart used, such as WedgePart.
  • The density of a part is determined by its Material or CustomPhysicalProperties, if specified.
m.s: Describes the mass of the part, the product of its density and volume.

kid.simple: Read-only. How heavy the part is: its volume times its density. Bigger parts and denser materials weigh more.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
print("This part weighs", part.Mass)

m.d:
If this property is enabled, the part will not contribute to the total mass or inertia of its assembly as long as it is welded to another part that has mass.

If the part is its own root part according to AssemblyRootPart, this will be ignored for that part, and it will still contribute mass and inertia to its assembly like a normal part. Parts that are massless should never become an assembly root part unless all other parts in the assembly are also massless.

This might be useful for things like optional accessories on vehicles that you don't want to affect the handling of the car or a massless render mesh welded to a simpler collision mesh.

See also Assemblies, an article documenting what root parts are and how to use them.
m.s: Determines whether the part contributes to the total mass or inertia of its rigid body.

kid.simple: If true, the part adds no weight to the assembly it is welded to. Useful for decorations on a car or a hat on a character, so they do not slow it down.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
part.Massless = true
kid.gotcha: It is ignored if this part is the assembly's root part or is not welded to anything with mass.

m.d:
The Material property allows you to set a part's texture and default physical properties (in the case that CustomPhysicalProperties is unset). The default Plastic material has a very light texture, while the SmoothPlastic material has no texture at all. Some material textures like DiamondPlate and Granite have very visible textures. Each material's texture reflects sunlight differently, especially Foil.

Setting this property then enabling CustomPhysicalProperties will use the default physical properties of a material. For instance, DiamondPlate is a very dense material while Wood is very light. A part's density determines whether it will float in terrain water.

The Glass material changes rendering behavior on moderate graphics settings by applying a bit of reflectiveness (similar to Reflectance) and perspective distortion. The effect is especially pronounced on sphere-shaped parts. Semi‑transparent parts behind Glass parts are not visible.
m.s: Determines the texture and default physical properties of a part.

kid.simple: What the part looks like it is made of (Plastic, Wood, Neon, Glass, Ice, and more). It also sets default physics, like how slippery Ice is.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
part.Material = Enum.Material.Neon -- glowing look

m.d: The system searches the MaterialVariant instance with the specified MaterialVariant name and Material type. If it successfully finds a matching MaterialVariant instance, it uses that instance to replace the default material. The default material can be the built-in material or an override MaterialVariant specified in MaterialService.
m.s: The name of `Class.MaterialVariant`.

kid.simple: The name of a custom material look (a MaterialVariant you made in MaterialService) to use instead of the built-in one.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
part.Material = Enum.Material.Brick
part.MaterialVariant = "MossyBrick" -- name of your MaterialVariant

m.d:
The Orientation property describes the part's rotation in degrees around the X, Y, and Z axes using a Vector3. The rotations are applied in Y ⟩ X ⟩ Z order. This differs from proper Euler angles and is instead Tait-Bryan angles which describe yaw, pitch, and roll.

It is also worth noting how this property differs from the CFrame.Angles() constructor which applies rotations in a different order (Z ⟩ Y ⟩ X). For better control over the rotation of a part, it's recommended that CFrame is set instead.

When setting this property, any Welds or Motor6Ds connected to this part will have the matching C0 or C1 property updated to allow the part to move relative to any other parts it is joined to. WeldConstraints will also be temporarily disabled and re-enabled during the move.
m.s: Describes the rotation of the part in the world.

kid.simple: Which way the part is turned, as three angles in degrees: around X (tip forward/back), around Y (spin left/right), around Z (roll sideways). (0, 0, 0) is not turned at all; (0, 90, 0) is spun a quarter turn around the up axis. Changing it turns the part in place without moving its center.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
part.Orientation = Vector3.new(0, 45, 0) -- spin 45 degrees
-- spin a little more every frame
while true do
	part.Orientation += Vector3.new(0, 2, 0)
	task.wait()
end
kid.gotcha: Orientation uses degrees but `CFrame.Angles` uses radians, and they apply the three turns in a different order. For exact control, use CFrame.

m.d:
This property specifies the offset of the part's pivot from its CFrame, that is BasePart:GetPivot() is the same as BasePart.CFrame multiplied by BasePart.PivotOffset.

This is convenient for setting the pivot to a location in local space, but setting a part's pivot to a location in world space can be done as follows:
m.s: Specifies the offset of the part's pivot from its `Datatype.CFrame`.

kid.simple: Where the part's pivot (its handle for `PivotTo`) sits, measured from the part's own center. Default is no offset, so the pivot is the center. GetPivot equals CFrame times PivotOffset.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local door = Workspace:WaitForChild("Door") -- 4 wide (X), 7 tall, 1 thick
-- Put the pivot on the door's left edge, 2 studs from the center, like a hinge
door.PivotOffset = CFrame.new(-2, 0, 0)
-- Now turning the pivot swings the door around its hinge
door:PivotTo(door:GetPivot() * CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(90), 0))

m.d:
The Position property describes the coordinates of a part using a Vector3. It reflects the position of the part's CFrame, however it can also be set.

When setting this property, any Welds or Motor6Ds connected to this part will have the matching C0 or C1 property updated to allow the part to move relative to any other parts it is joined to. WeldConstraints will also be temporarily disabled and re-enabled during the move.
m.s: Describes the position of the part in the world.

kid.simple: Where the center of the part is, as (X, Y, Z) in studs from the center of the map. (0, 5, 0) is 5 studs straight up. Setting it moves the part without turning it.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 5, 0)
-- move by an offset of (2, 0, 0): now at (2, 5, 0)
part.Position += Vector3.new(2, 0, 0)
print(part.Position) --> 2, 5, 0
kid.gotcha: Position always matches `CFrame.Position`. Changing one changes the other.

m.d: Indicates the time in seconds since the part's physics were last updated on the local client or the server. This value will be 0 when the part has no physics (Anchored is true).
m.s: Time since last recorded physics update.

kid.simple: Read-only. How many seconds since this part's physics was last updated on this computer. It is 0 for anchored parts.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
print(part.ReceiveAge)

m.d:
The Reflectance property determines how much a part reflects the sky. A value of 0 indicates the part is not reflective at all, and a value of 1 indicates the part should fully reflect.

Reflectance is not affected by Transparency unless the part is fully transparent, in which case reflectance will not render at all. Reflectance may or may not be ignored depending on the Material of the part.
m.s: Determines how much a part reflects the skybox.

kid.simple: How shiny and mirror-like the part is, from 0 (not shiny) to 1 (fully reflects the sky).
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
part.Reflectance = 0.8 -- very shiny

m.d:
The ResizeableFaces property uses a Faces object to describe the different faces on which a part may be resized. For most implementations of BasePart, such as Part and WedgePart, this property includes all faces. However, TrussPart will set its ResizeableFaces set to only two faces since those kinds of parts must have two Size dimensions of length 2.

This property is most commonly used with tools for building and manipulating parts and has little use outside of that context. The Handles class, which has the Handles.Faces property, can be used in conjunction with this property to display only the handles on faces that can be resized on a part.
m.s: Describes the faces on which a part may be resized.

kid.simple: Read-only. Which faces of the part can be resized. Most parts allow all six; TrussPart only allows two.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
print(part.ResizeableFaces)

m.d: The ResizeIncrement property is a read-only property that describes the smallest change in size allowable by the Resize() method. It differs between implementations of the BasePart abstract class; for instance, Part has this set to 1 while TrussPart has this set to 2 since individual truss sections are 2×2×2 in size.
m.s: Describes the smallest change in size allowable by the `Class.BasePart:Resize()|Resize()` method.

kid.simple: Read-only. The smallest step `Resize` can change the part by. It is 1 stud for a Part and 2 for a TrussPart.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
print(part.ResizeIncrement) --> 1

m.s: Determines the second parameter for the SurfaceType on the Right face of a part.

m.s: Determines the type of surface for the right face of a part.

kid.simple: The surface style of the part's right face (the +X side), like Smooth or Studs. Some old surface types could join touching parts together; today most builders leave it Smooth.
kid.example:

The RightSurfaceInput property determines the kind of input provided to a

  • For Sin, the motor rotates at a velocity equal to ParamA * math.sin(workspace.DistributedGameTime * ParamB). See Workspace.DistributedGameTime.
m.s: Determines the kind of input for the Right face of a part (-X direction).

m.d:
This property is an integer between -127 and 127 that takes precedence over all other rules for root part sort. When considering multiple parts that are not Anchored and which share the same Massless value, a part with a higher RootPriority will take priority over those with lower RootPriority.

You can use this property to control which part of an assembly is the root part and keep the root part stable if size changes.

See also Assemblies, an article documenting what root parts are and how to use them.
m.s: The main rule in determining the root part of an assembly.

kid.simple: A number from -127 to 127. In a group of welded parts, the one with the highest RootPriority is picked as the root (main) part. Most games leave it at 0.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
part.RootPriority = 10

m.d:
The rotation of the part in degrees for the three axes.

When setting this property, any Welds or Motor6Ds connected to this part will have the matching C0 or C1 property updated to allow the part to move relative to any other parts it is joined to. WeldConstraints will also be temporarily disabled and re-enabled during the move.
m.s: The rotation of the part in degrees for the three axes.

kid.simple: Another way to read or set the part's turn in degrees for the X, Y, and Z axes. It applies the three turns in a different order than Orientation, so the numbers can differ. Most people use Orientation or CFrame instead.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
part.Rotation = Vector3.new(0, 90, 0)
print(part.Orientation)

m.d:
The RotVelocity of a part describes how its BasePart.Orientation is presently changing. In other words, this property describes how the fast part is rotating. The part only rotates if it is not anchored.

The unit of this property is radians per second.

Using this in conjunction with AlignOrientation allows for aligned parts to have matching RotVelocity and Orientation values.
m.s: Determines a part's change in orientation over time.
m.dep: This property is deprecated. Use AssemblyAngularVelocity instead.

kid.simple: Old — use `AssemblyAngularVelocity` instead.

m.d:
A part's Size property determines its visual dimensions, while ExtentsSize represents the actual size used by the physics engine, such as in collision detection. The individual dimensions (length, height, width) can be as low as 0.001 and as high as 2048. Size dimensions below 0.05 will be physically simulated as if the part's dimensions are 0.05, while visual rendering preserves the actual size.

A part's Size is used in a variety of additional ways:

  • To influence its mass as given by GetMass().
  • By ParticleEmitter to determine the area from which particles are spawned.
  • By BlockMesh to partially determine the rendered rectangular prism.
  • By SpecialMesh for certain MeshTypes to determine the size of the rendered mesh.
  • By SurfaceLight to determine the space to illuminate.
m.s: Determines the dimensions of a part (length, height, width).

kid.simple: How big the part is: (width X, height Y, depth Z) in studs. A default Part is (4, 1, 2). Each side can be from 0.001 up to 2048 studs.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
part.Size = Vector3.new(10, 1, 10) -- a flat 10 by 10 platform
kid.gotcha: Changing Size keeps the center in the same place, so a part grows in both directions. Grow its height by 4 and its bottom moves down 2.

m.d:
The TopSurfaceInput property determines the kind of input provided to a part's BasePart.TopSurface. This is only relevant for Motor or SteppingMotor SurfaceTypes. This property determines how BasePart.TopParamA and BasePart.TopParamB are used. For brevity, these properties will be referred to as ParamA and ParamB, respectively.

  • By default, this is set to NoInput. This stops the motor altogether,
  • For Constant, the motor rotates at a constant velocity equal to ParamB.
  • For Sin, the motor rotates at a velocity equal to ParamA * math.sin(workspace.DistributedGameTime * ParamB). See Workspace.DistributedGameTime.
m.s: Determines the kind of input for the Top face of a part (+Y direction).
m.dep: Deprecated.

kid.simple: Old — old surface settings that no longer do anything. You do not need it.

m.d:
The Transparency property controls the visibility of a part on a scale of 0 to 1 where 0 is completely visible (opaque) and 1 is completely invisible (not rendered at all).

While fully transparent parts are not rendered at all, partially transparent objects have some significant rendering costs. Having many translucent parts may impact performance.

When transparent parts overlap, render order may act unpredictably, so you should avoid semi-transparent parts from overlapping.

See also LocalTransparencyModifier as a multiplier to Transparency that's only visible to the local client.
m.s: Determines how much a part can be seen through (the inverse of part opacity).

kid.simple: How see-through the part is, from 0 (solid) to 1 (completely invisible). 0.5 is half see-through.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
-- fade out over 1 second
for t = 0, 1, 0.1 do
	part.Transparency = t
	task.wait(0.1)
end
kid.gotcha: An invisible part can still be bumped into. Also set CanCollide to false for a fully ghostly part.

m.d:
The Velocity of a part describes how its BasePart.Position is presently changing. The unit of this property is studs per second. For reference, the default Roblox character moves at 16 studs per second via Humanoid.WalkSpeed. The acceleration due to gravity is found in Workspace.Gravity (by default, -196.2 studs per second per second).

Setting the Velocity of a part that is BasePart.Anchored will cause it to act like a conveyor belt. Any object that touches the part will begin to move in accordance with the Velocity.

Some BodyMover objects will apply forces and thus change the Velocity of a part over time. The simplest of these is a BodyForce which can be used to counteract the acceleration due to gravity on a single part (set the +Y axis of the BodyForce.Force to the product of the mass (BasePart:GetMass()) and the gravity constant).
m.s: Determines a part's change in position over time.
m.dep: This property is deprecated. Use AssemblyLinearVelocity instead.

kid.simple: Old — use `AssemblyLinearVelocity` instead.

m.d:
Returns the world-space torque vector that must be applied to the part's assembly to achieve the specified angular acceleration. This result can be used to determine the torque that should be applied via a Torque instance or BasePart:ApplyAngularImpulse().

The calculation uses Euler's rotation equation where I is the assembly's world-space inertia tensor, α is the desired angular acceleration, and ω is the angular velocity.

τ = I · α + ω × (I · ω)

If the part is not a descendant of Workspace, this method returns a vector of infinity. If the assembly is anchored, it similarly returns a vector of infinity.

Gyroscopic Effects

When a spinning assembly has an asymmetric inertia tensor, the torque required to achieve a specified angular acceerlation is augmented due to the changing orientation of the body. The optional angVelocity parameter accounts for these gyroscopic effects. If omitted, these gyroscopic effects are omitted from the calculation.
m.s: Returns the torque needed to achieve a given angular acceleration on this part's assembly, optionally accounting for gyroscopic effects.

p.s: The desired angular acceleration vector in world space.
The current angular velocity of the assembly in world space. Defaults to (0, 0, 0). Supply the assembly's angular velocity to account for gyroscopic effects.

r.s: A Vector3 representing the world-space torque required to produce the specified angular acceleration.

kid.simple: Advanced physics. Tells you how much twisting force (torque) you need to make the assembly speed up its spin by the amount you want.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
local torque = part:AngularAccelerationToTorque(Vector3.new(0, 5, 0))
print("Torque needed:", torque)

m.d:
Applies an instant angular force impulse to this part's assembly, causing the assembly to spin.

The resulting angular velocity from the impulse relies on the assembly's mass. So a higher impulse is required to move more massive assemblies. Impulses are useful for cases where you want a force applied instantly, such as an explosion or collision.

If the part is owned by the server, this function must be called from a server Script (not from a LocalScript or a Script with RunContext set to RunContext.Client). If the part is owned by a client through automatic ownership, this function can be called from either a client script or a server script; calling it from a client script for a server-owned part will have no effect.
m.s: Apply an angular impulse to the assembly.

p.s: An angular impulse vector to be applied to the assembly.

kid.simple: Gives the assembly a sudden twist, making it start spinning. Heavier things spin less from the same twist.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
part.Anchored = false
part:ApplyAngularImpulse(Vector3.new(0, 500, 0)) -- spin around the up axis
kid.gotcha: Only works where the part's physics is run (its network owner). For parts owned by the server, call it from a server Script.

m.d:
This function applies an instant force impulse to this part's assembly.

The force is applied at the assembly's center of mass, so the resulting movement will only be linear.

The resulting velocity from the impulse relies on the assembly's mass. So a higher impulse is required to move more massive assemblies. Impulses are useful for cases where you want a force applied instantly, such as an explosion or collision.

If the part is owned by the server, this function must be called from a server Script (not from a LocalScript or a Script with RunContext set to RunContext.Client). If the part is owned by a client through automatic ownership, this function can be called from either a client script or a server script; calling it from a client script for a server-owned part will have no effect.
m.s: Apply an impulse to the assembly at the assembly's `Class.BasePart.AssemblyCenterOfMass|center of mass`.

p.s: A linear impulse vector to be applied to the assembly.

kid.simple: Gives the assembly a sudden shove, like a kick, through its balance point, so it moves without spinning. Heavier things move slower from the same shove. Multiply by AssemblyMass to get the same speed for any weight.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
part.Anchored = false
-- add about 50 studs/second of upward speed, whatever it weighs
part:ApplyImpulse(Vector3.new(0, 50 * part.AssemblyMass, 0))
kid.gotcha: Only works where the part's physics is run (its network owner). For a player's character, the player's device owns it, so call it from a LocalScript.

m.d:
This function applies an instant force impulse to this part's assembly, at the specified position in world space.

If the position is not at the assembly's center of mass, the impulse will cause a positional and rotational movement.

The resulting velocity from the impulse relies on the assembly's mass. So a higher impulse is required to move more massive assemblies. Impulses are useful for cases where developers want a force applied instantly, such as an explosion or collision.

If the part is owned by the server, this function must be called from a server Script (not from a LocalScript or a Script with RunContext set to RunContext.Client). If the part is owned by a client through automatic ownership, this function can be called from either a client script or a server script; calling it from a client script for a server-owned part will have no effect.
m.s: Apply an impulse to the assembly at specified position.

p.s: An impulse vector to be applied to the assembly.
The position, in world space, to apply the impulse.

kid.simple: Gives the assembly a sudden shove at a specific world position. Hitting off-center makes it both move AND spin, like kicking the edge of a box.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
part.Anchored = false
-- push sideways at the top edge so it tips over
local topEdge = part.Position + Vector3.new(0, part.Size.Y / 2, 0)
part:ApplyImpulseAtPosition(Vector3.new(100, 0, 0), topEdge)

m.d:
Subscribes callback to the contact data that the physics engine generates for this part while detecting collisions. Once per frame, after the simulation has stepped, callback receives an array of summaries describing every contact patch this part was involved in during that frame. Each summary reports where the contact occurred, which direction it faced, and how fast the two parts were moving relative to each other at that point.

This method is a separate mechanism from BasePart.Touched.

Throws an error if callback is nil, or if the part is not a descendant of Workspace.

Summary Fields

Each entry in the array passed to callback is a table with the following keys:

Key Type Summary
Time number Simulation time, in seconds, of the physics substep that produced this summary.
Part0 Class.BasePart The subscribed part.
Part1 Class.BasePart The other part in the pair, which may be Class.Terrain.
Point Datatype.Vector3 Contact point in world space, averaged across the points in the patch.
Normal Datatype.Vector3 Unit contact normal for the patch, oriented relative to the subscribed part.
RelativeVelocity Datatype.Vector3 Velocity of Part1 relative to Part0 at the contact point.
Area number Estimated area of the contact patch, in square studs. 0 for a patch of fewer than three points, such as an edge or corner contact.

Normal is oriented relative to the subscribed part rather than to whichever part the engine happened to list first, so if both parts of a pair are subscribed, each subscription receives its own summary with itself as Part0 and the normal flipped to match.

RelativeVelocity is the velocity of Part1 relative to Part0, so the magnitude of its projection onto Normal is the speed at which the two parts are approaching or separating head-on, and the component tangential to Normal describes sliding and glancing contact.

Reporting Behavior

  • Contact recording is enabled only while at least one subscription exists anywhere in the Workspace, and the cost of it scales with the number of subscribed parts rather than with the total number of collisions in the scene.
  • Contacts between multiple sleeping parts do not produce summaries.
  • Contacts from Parts with BasePart.CanCollide set to false do not produce summaries.
  • Physics may run several substeps per frame, so a pair that stays in contact across several of them produces up to one summary per patch per substep, all delivered in the same invocation of callback. Use Time to order them.
  • Non-convex collision geometry produces one summary per pair of touching convex hulls, and contact with Terrain is split further by contact normal, so either can yield several summaries for the same pair within one substep.
  • Nothing is replicated. Each client generates summaries for the collisions it owns. See network ownership.
  • Destroying the part disconnects its subscriptions.
m.s: Subscribes to detailed per-frame contact data for the collisions this part is involved in.

p.s: Invoked with an array of summary tables, at most once per frame, if the part was involved in a collision.

r.s: A RBXScriptConnection that ends the subscription when disconnected.

kid.simple: Advanced. Hands your function a detailed report every frame about each contact this part had: where it touched, the direction, and how fast the parts hit. It returns a connection you can Disconnect later.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
local connection = part:BindToCollisionSummaries(function(summaries)
	for _, s in summaries do
		print("Hit", s.Part1.Name, "at", s.Point)
	end
end)
task.wait(10)
connection:Disconnect() -- stop listening
kid.gotcha: Errors if the part is not in Workspace. It is separate from the Touched event.

m.d: Returns whether the parts can collide with each other or not. This function takes into account the collision groups of the two parts. This function will error if the specified part is not a BasePart.
m.s: Returns whether the parts can collide with each other.

p.s: The specified part being checked for collidability.

r.s: Whether the parts can collide with each other.

kid.simple: Gives true if this part and another part are allowed to bump into each other, checking their collision groups.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local a = Workspace:WaitForChild("PartA")
local b = Workspace:WaitForChild("PartB")
print(a:CanCollideWith(b))

m.d:
The CanSetNetworkOwnership function checks whether you can set a part's network ownership.

The function's return value verifies whether or not you can call BasePart:SetNetworkOwner() or BasePart:SetNetworkOwnershipAuto() without encountering an error. It returns true if you can modify/read the network ownership, or returns false and the reason you can't, as a string.
m.s: Checks whether you can set a part's network ownership.

r.s: Whether you can modify or read the network ownership and the reason.

m.d:
Returns a table of parts connected to the object by any kind of rigid joint.

If recursive is true this function will return all of the parts in the assembly rigidly connected to the BasePart.

Rigid Joints

When a joint connects two parts together (Part0 → Part1), a joint is rigid if the physics of Part1 are completely locked down by Part0. This only applies to the following joint types:

  • Weld
  • Snap
  • ManualWeld
  • Motor
  • Motor6D
  • WeldConstraint
m.s: Returns a table of parts connected to the object by any kind of rigid joint.

p.s: A table of parts connected to the object by any kind of joint.

r.s: An array of BaseParts connected to this part by rigid joints. If recursive is true, includes all parts in the assembly.

kid.simple: Gives a list of parts stuck to this one by rigid joints (like welds). Pass true to get every part in the whole welded group.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
for _, other in part:GetConnectedParts(true) do
	print(other.Name)
end

m.d:
Returns an array of all Joints and Constraints connected to this part that are active in the simulation.

A joint or constraint only becomes active once both of the parts it connects are inside the same simulated container, such as Workspace or a WorldModel. If one of the connected parts is outside that container — for example, parented to ServerStorage, or in a different WorldModel — the joint is not activated. GetJoints() does not include that joint on either part, even though the joint instance still exists in the data model.
m.s: Returns all Joints or Constraints connected to this part that are active in the simulation.

r.s: An array of all Joints and Constraints connected to the part that are active in the simulation.

kid.simple: Gives a list of all joints and constraints (like welds and hinges) connected to this part that are currently active.

m.d:
Creates a new IntersectOperation from the intersecting geometry of the part and the other parts in the given array. Only Parts are supported, not Terrain or MeshParts. Similar to Clone(), the returned object has no set Parent.

The following properties from the calling part are applied to the resulting IntersectOperation:

  • Color, Material, MaterialVariant, Reflectance, Transparency
  • CanCollide
  • Anchored, Density, Elasticity, ElasticityWeight, Friction, FrictionWeight

Migration

It is highly recommended to use the newer GeometryService:IntersectAsync() instead of this method. As well as having better performance and more features, the new method differs as follows:

  • The output is an array of instances rather than a single instance.
  • The input parts do not need to be parented to the scene, allowing for background operations.
  • When the SplitApart option is set to true (default), each distinct body will be returned in its own PartOperation.
  • All the returned parts are in the coordinate space of the main part, so their PVInstance.Origin positions are the same as the main part's. This keeps the vertices of the mesh in the same position relative to the object as before the operation, but it does also mean the (0, 0, 0) of a returned part is not necessarily at the center of its body.

Notes

  • The original parts remain intact following a successful intersect operation. In most cases, you should Destroy() all of the original parts and parent the returned IntersectOperation to the same place as the calling BasePart.
  • By default, the face colors of the resulting intersection are borrowed from the Color property of the original parts. To change the entire intersection to a specific color, set its UsePartColor property to true.
  • If an intersect operation would result in a part with more than 20,000 triangles, it will be simplified to 20,000 triangles.
m.s: Creates a new `Class.IntersectOperation` from the overlapping geometry of the part and the other parts in the given array.

p.s: The objects taking part in the intersection.
The CollisionFidelity value for the resulting IntersectOperation.
The RenderFidelity value of the resulting PartOperation.

r.s: Resulting IntersectOperation with default name Intersect.

kid.simple: Makes a new shape from only the parts where this part and the others OVERLAP, like the shared middle of two circles.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local base = Workspace:WaitForChild("Base")
local other = Workspace:WaitForChild("Other")
local ok, result = pcall(function()
	return base:IntersectAsync({other})
end)
if ok and result then
	result.Parent = Workspace -- new shape starts with no Parent
	base:Destroy()
	other:Destroy()
end
kid.gotcha: It yields (waits) and can fail, so wrap it in pcall. Only Parts work, not MeshParts or Terrain. The result has no Parent until you set one.

m.d:
Creates a joint on any side of the Part that has a SurfaceType that can make a joint it will create a joint with any adjacent parts.

Joints will be created between the sides and any planar touching surfaces, depending on the sides' surfaces.

  • Smooth surfaces will not create joints
  • Glue surfaces will create a Glue joint
  • Weld will create a Weld joint with any surface except for Unjoinable
  • Studs, Inlet, or Universal will each create a Snap joint with either of other the other two surfaces (e.g. Studs with Inlet and Universal)
  • Hinge and Motor surfaces create Rotate and RotateV joint instances

Unlike Model:MakeJoints(), this function requires an array of parts as a parameter. This array is given as follows:

part:MakeJoints({part1, part2, part3})

Joints are broken if enough force is applied to them due to an Explosion, unless a ForceField object is parented to the BasePart or ancestor Model. For this reason, they are often used to make simple destructible buildings and other models.
m.s: Creates a joint on any side of the object that has a surface ID that can make a joint.
m.dep: SurfaceType based joining is deprecated, do not use MakeJoints for new projects. WeldConstraints and HingeConstraints should be used instead.

kid.simple: Old — use WeldConstraint objects to join parts instead.

m.d: Sets the given player as network owner for this and all connected parts. When playerInstance is nil, the server will be the owner instead of a player.
m.s: Sets the given player as network owner for this and all connected parts.

p.s: The player being given network ownership of the part.

kid.simple: Server only. Chooses which player's device runs this part's physics (and everything welded to it). Pass nil to make the server run it. Giving a player ownership of their own car makes driving feel smooth.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

	local humanoid = seat.Occupant
	if humanoid then
		local player = Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(humanoid.Parent)
		seat:SetNetworkOwner(player)
	else

	end
end)

m.d:
Returns the world-space angular acceleration that would result from applying the specified torque to the part's assembly, optionally taking into account gyroscopic effects.

This is the inverse of BasePart:AngularAccelerationToTorque(). It is useful for predicting how an assembly will respond to an applied torque.

The calculation uses:

α = I⁻¹ · (τ − ω × (I · ω))

where I is the assembly's world-space inertia tensor, τ is the applied torque, and ω is the angular velocity.

If the part is not a descendant of Workspace, returns (0, 0, 0). If the assembly is anchored, returns (0, 0, 0).

Gyroscopic Effects

When a spinning assembly has an asymmetric inertia tensor, the acceleration resulting from an applied torque also depends on the current angular velocity. The angVelocity parameter accounts for these gyroscopic effects. If omitted (defaults to zero), the result neglects this contribution from the result.
m.s: Returns the angular acceleration that would result from applying a given torque to this part's assembly, optionally accounting for gyroscopic effects.

p.s: The torque vector applied to the assembly in world space.
The current angular velocity of the assembly in world space. Defaults to (0, 0, 0). Supply the assembly's angular velocity to account for gyroscopic effects.

r.s: A Vector3 representing the resulting angular acceleration in world space.

kid.simple: Advanced physics. The opposite of AngularAccelerationToTorque: tells you how much faster the assembly would start spinning if you applied a given twisting force.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Workspace:WaitForChild("Part")
print(part:TorqueToAngularAcceleration(Vector3.new(0, 1000, 0)))
