m.d:
The Touched event fires when a part comes in contact with another part. For instance, if PartA bumps into PartB, then PartA.Touched fires with PartB, and PartB.Touched fires with PartA.

This event only fires as a result of physical movement, so it will not fire if the CFrame property was changed such that the part overlaps another part. This also means that at least one of the parts involved must not be Anchored at the time of the collision.

This event works in conjunction with Workspace.TouchesUseCollisionGroups to specify whether collision groups are acknowledged for detection.
m.s: Fires when a part touches another part as a result of physical movement.

p.s: The other part that came in contact with the given part.

kid.simple: Fires when another part bumps into this one because of physics movement. It gives you the other part. This is how lava, coins, checkpoints, and buttons on the floor usually work.
kid.example:
-- Script inside a coin Part
local coin = script.Parent
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local taken = false

coin.Touched:Connect(function(otherPart)
	local player = Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(otherPart.Parent)
	if player and not taken then
		taken = true
		print(player.Name, "got the coin!")
		coin:Destroy()
	end
end)
kid.gotcha: It does not fire if a part was simply teleported into another by setting CFrame, and at least one of the two parts must be unanchored. It often fires many times quickly, so use a flag like `taken` (a debounce).

end)

kid.simple: BasePart is the family of all the solid 3D blocks you build with: Part, MeshPart, WedgePart, SpawnLocation, and more. Anything in this family can be seen, can bump into things, and can fall with gravity when it is inside Workspace. It gives every part its position, rotation, size, color, material, and physics settings, plus the Touched event.
kid.analogy: BasePart is like the word "vehicle". Cars, bikes, and buses are all vehicles and all have wheels and a speed. In the same way, Part and MeshPart are both BaseParts, and both have Position, Size, Color, Anchored, and so on.
whenToUse: Move or turn a part with `Position`, `Orientation`, or `CFrame`.
Change how a part looks with `Color`, `Material`, `Transparency`, and `Size`.
Freeze a part in place with `Anchored`, or let things walk through it with `CanCollide = false`.
Make something happen when a player steps on a part with the `Touched` event.
Push or launch a part with physics using `ApplyImpulse` or `AssemblyLinearVelocity`.
kid.where: Parts only show up and do physics when they are inside Workspace. You get BasePart members on any Part, MeshPart, etc. You cannot create a plain BasePart; use `Instance.new("Part")` instead. Works in both Scripts and LocalScripts, but changes made in a LocalScript are only seen by that one player.

terms.stud: Roblox's unit of distance. A default Part is 4 studs long, 1 stud tall, and 2 studs wide.
terms.Vector3: Three numbers (X, Y, Z) in one value. Used for positions, sizes, and directions. X is left/right, Y is up/down, Z is forward/back.
terms.Position: WHERE the center of the part is, as a Vector3 measured from the center of the map (0, 0, 0). (0, 5, 0) means 5 studs straight up from the center.
terms.Orientation: WHICH WAY the part is turned, as three angles in degrees: (turn around X, turn around Y, turn around Z). (0, 90, 0) means spun 90 degrees around the up-and-down axis, like turning to face a different wall.
terms.CFrame: Short for coordinate frame. One value that holds BOTH Position and rotation together. Setting CFrame moves and turns the part in one step.
terms.pivot: The handle point you move the part by with `PivotTo`. By default it is the part's center, so the pivot equals the CFrame. `PivotOffset` can move the handle, for example to the bottom of the part.
terms.world space: Measuring from the center of the map. World X always points the same way no matter how the part is turned.
terms.local space (object space): Measuring from the part itself, using the part's own front, up, and right directions. 5 studs forward in local space depends on which way the part faces.
terms.offset: An amount you add to shift something. A part at (0, 5, 0) moved by an offset of (2, 0, 0) ends up at (2, 5, 0).
terms.degrees / radians: Two ways to measure turning. A full turn is 360 degrees or about 6.28 radians. Orientation uses degrees; `CFrame.Angles` uses radians, so convert with `math.rad(90)`.
terms.physics: The game's built-in rules for gravity, falling, bouncing, and pushing.
terms.anchored: Frozen in place. Physics will not move it, but scripts still can.
terms.collide: To bump into something instead of passing through it.
terms.assembly: A group of parts stuck together (for example by welds) that physics moves as one piece. A single loose part is an assembly of one.
terms.velocity: Speed plus direction. (0, 50, 0) means moving straight up at 50 studs per second.
terms.angular velocity: How fast something is spinning, and around which axis, measured in radians per second.
terms.impulse: A sudden one-time push, like a kick. Bigger impulse means a harder push; heavier things need a bigger push to go the same speed.
terms.torque: A twisting push that makes something spin.
terms.mass: How heavy a part is. It equals its volume times its density (how packed the material is).
terms.center of mass: The balance point of a part or assembly.
terms.network owner: Which computer runs the physics for a part: the server, or one player's device. Roblox usually picks this automatically.
terms.server / client: The server is Roblox's computer running the game for everyone. A client is one player's own device.
terms.replicate: To copy a change from the server to every player's device so everyone sees it.
terms.spatial query: A search for parts in an area, like a raycast (shooting an invisible laser) or checking what is inside a box.
terms.collision group: A named team of parts. You can set rules like "parts in Ghosts never collide with parts in Walls".
terms.joint / weld: Something that connects two parts so they move together.
terms.yield: To pause the script and wait. Methods ending in Async yield until they finish.
terms.deprecated: Old and replaced by something newer. Use the new version instead.
terms.event: Something that announces "this just happened!". Use `:Connect(function)` to run code each time.

examples.title: Position vs Orientation vs CFrame vs Pivot (with numbers)
examples.code:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Anchored = true
part.Size = Vector3.new(4, 4, 4)
part.Parent = Workspace

-- 1) POSITION = where the CENTER is (in studs from the map center)
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 5, 0)
-- Move it by an offset of (2, 0, 0): it ends at (2, 5, 0)
part.Position = part.Position + Vector3.new(2, 0, 0)
print(part.Position)        --> 2, 5, 0

-- 2) ORIENTATION = which way it is turned, in DEGREES (X, Y, Z)
part.Orientation = Vector3.new(0, 90, 0) -- spun 90 degrees around the up axis
print(part.Orientation)     --> 0, 90, 0
print(part.Position)        --> 2, 5, 0 (turning did not move it)

-- 3) CFRAME = position AND rotation together in one value
-- Put it at (10, 5, 0) and face it 90 degrees to the left, in one step
part.CFrame = CFrame.new(10, 5, 0) * CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(90), 0)
print(part.Position)        --> 10, 5, 0  (Position always matches CFrame.Position)

-- Move 5 studs FORWARD in the direction the part is facing (local space)
-- It faces -X now, so (10, 5, 0) becomes (5, 5, 0)
part.CFrame = part.CFrame * CFrame.new(0, 0, -5)
print(part.Position)        --> 5, 5, 0

-- 4) PIVOT = the handle used by GetPivot/PivotTo (default: the center)
print(part:GetPivot() == part.CFrame) --> true
-- Move the handle to the BOTTOM of the 4-stud-tall part (2 studs down)
part.PivotOffset = CFrame.new(0, -2, 0)
-- Put the bottom on the floor at (20, 0, 0); the center ends up at (20, 2, 0)
part:PivotTo(CFrame.new(20, 0, 0))
print(part.Position)        --> 20, 2, 0
explain: Position is just WHERE the center is. Adding (2, 0, 0) slides it 2 studs along the world X axis, from (0, 5, 0) to (2, 5, 0).
Orientation is just WHICH WAY it is turned, in degrees. Changing it spins the part in place; the Position stays the same.
CFrame is both at once. `CFrame.new(10, 5, 0)` is the spot, and `* CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(90), 0)` turns it 90 degrees. Reading `part.Position` afterward always gives the CFrame's position.

`part.CFrame * CFrame.new(0, 0, -5)` means "5 studs in front of where the part is facing". Forward for a part is its -Z direction. Because the part was turned to face -X, forward is toward smaller X, so it goes from (10, 5, 0) to (5, 5, 0).

The pivot is the handle. At first it is the center, so `GetPivot()` equals CFrame. After setting `PivotOffset` 2 studs down, the handle is at the bottom face. `PivotTo(CFrame.new(20, 0, 0))` puts that bottom at (20, 0, 0), so the center sits at (20, 2, 0).

examples.title: Lava floor that hurts players
examples.place: Script inside a Part in Workspace
examples.code:
local lava = script.Parent
lava.Anchored = true
lava.Color = Color3.fromRGB(255, 80, 0)
lava.Material = Enum.Material.Neon

lava.Touched:Connect(function(otherPart)
	-- otherPart is the thing that touched the lava (like a foot)
	local character = otherPart.Parent
	local humanoid = character:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
	if humanoid then
		humanoid.Health = 0
	end
end)
explain: We make the part anchored (frozen), orange, and glowing.
`Touched` fires whenever something bumps into it, and gives us that part.
A body part's Parent is the character model. If it has a Humanoid, it is a player or NPC, so we set its Health to 0.

examples.title: Launch pad
examples.place: Script inside an anchored Part in Workspace
examples.code:
local pad = script.Parent
local cooldown = {} -- remember who was just launched

pad.Touched:Connect(function(otherPart)
	local character = otherPart.Parent
	local humanoid = character:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
	local root = character:FindFirstChild("HumanoidRootPart")
	if humanoid and root and not cooldown[character] then
		cooldown[character] = true
		-- Set the speed straight up to 100 studs per second
		root.AssemblyLinearVelocity = Vector3.new(0, 100, 0)
		task.wait(1)
		cooldown[character] = nil
	end
end)
explain: Touched can fire many times per step, so a cooldown table stops it from launching the same character over and over.
HumanoidRootPart is the main part of a character. Setting its `AssemblyLinearVelocity` to (0, 100, 0) shoots the whole character upward at 100 studs per second.
After 1 second the character can be launched again.

gotchas: Parts fall unless `Anchored` is true. If your new part vanishes, it probably fell through the map or out of the world.
`CFrame.Angles` uses radians, but `Orientation` uses degrees. Use `math.rad(degrees)` when building a CFrame.
To move a whole Model, use `model:PivotTo(...)`, not each part's Position.
`Touched` only fires from physics movement. If you teleport a part into another by setting CFrame, Touched does not fire. Also, two anchored parts never touch each other.
`Touched` fires a lot (every body part, many times). Use a cooldown (debounce) so your code runs once.
`CanCollide = false` on an unanchored part makes it fall through the floor.
Changes made in a LocalScript (like color) are only seen by that player. Use a server Script for changes everyone should see.

class/BaseRemoteEvent.d:
Abstract base class inherited by RemoteEvent and UnreliableRemoteEvent. It defines shared behavior for asynchronous, one-way communication across the client-server boundary without yielding for a response — from a client to the server, from the server to a specific client, or from the server to all clients.

This class isn't creatable. Use RemoteEvent for reliable, ordered delivery, or UnreliableRemoteEvent when reduced latency and network traffic matter more than guaranteed delivery. Fire and receive APIs (FireServer, FireClient, FireAllClients, OnServerEvent, OnClientEvent) are defined on those subclasses. If you need a return value, use a RemoteFunction instead.

class/Beam.d:
A Beam object connects two Attachments by drawing a texture between them.

To display, a beam must be a descendant of the Workspace with its Attachment0 and Attachment1 properties set to Attachments also descending from the Workspace.

The beam's appearance can be customized using the range of properties outlined below. Also see the Beams guide for visual examples.

Beam Curvature

Beams are configured to use a cubic Bézier curve formed by four control points. This means they are not constrained to straight lines and the curve of the beam can be modified by changing CurveSize0, CurveSize1, and the orientation of the beam's Attachments.

  • P0 — The start of the beam; position of Attachment0.
  • P1 — CurveSize0 studs away from Attachment0, in the positive X direction of Attachment0.
  • P2 — CurveSize1 studs away from Attachment1, in the negative X direction of Attachment1.
  • P3 — The end of the beam; position of Attachment1
class/Beam.s: Connects two `Class.Attachment|Attachments` by drawing a texture between them.

m.d:
The Attachment the beam originates from. This attachment is the first control point on the beam's cubic Bézier curve; its orientation, alongside the CurveSize0 property, determines the position of the second control point. See Beams for more details.

For the Attachment where the beam ends, see Attachment1.
m.s: The `Class.Attachment` the beam originates from.

m.d:
The Attachment the beam ends at. This attachment is the fourth and final control point on the beam's cubic Bézier curve; its orientation, alongside the CurveSize1 property, determines the position of the third control point. See Beams for more details.

For the Attachment where the beam originates from, see Attachment0.
m.s: The `Class.Attachment` the beam ends at.

m.d: Scales the light emitted from the beam when LightInfluence is less than 1. This property is 1 by default and can set to any number within the range of 0 to 10000. Increasing the value of LightInfluence decreases the effect of this property's value.
m.s: Scales the light emitted from the beam when `Class.Beam.LightInfluence|LightInfluence` is less than 1.

m.d:
Determines the color of the beam across its Segments. If Texture is set, this color will be applied to the beam's texture. If no Texture is set, the Beam will appear as a solid line colored in accordance with this property.

This property is a ColorSequence, allowing the color to be configured to vary across the length of the beam. Consider the following ColorSequence which, when applied to a beam, would yield the pictured result.

local colorSequence = ColorSequence.new({
        ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(0, Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0)), -- Red
        ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(0.5, Color3.fromRGB(0, 188, 203)), -- Cyan
        ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(1, Color3.fromRGB(196, 0, 255)), -- Purple
    }
)

Note the beam's coloration also depends on the number of Segments the Beam has. Each segment of the beam can only show a transition between two colors. Therefore a Beam will need to have at least n-1 segments in order for the color to display correctly, where n is the number of ColorSequenceKeypoints in the ColorSequence.
m.s: Determines the color of the beam across its `Class.Beam.Segments|Segments`.

m.d:
Determines, along with Attachment0, the position of the second control point in the beam's Bézier curve. See Beams for more details.

m.s: Determines, along with `Class.Beam.Attachment0|Attachment0`, the position of the second control point in the beam's Bézier curve.

Determines, along with Attachment1, the position of the third control point in the beam's Bézier curve. See Beams for more details.

The position of this point can be determined by the following equation:
m.s: Determines, along with `Class.Beam.Attachment1|Attachment1`, the position of the third control point in the beam's Bézier curve.

Determines whether the beam is visible or not.

When this property is set to false, the beam's Segments will not be displayed.
m.s: Determines whether the beam is visible or not.

m.d: A Beam is a 2D projection existing in 3D space, meaning that it may not be visible from every angle. The FaceCamera property, when set to true, ensures that the beam always faces the CurrentCamera, regardless of its orientation.
m.s: Determines whether the `Class.Beam.Segments|Segments` of the beam will always face the camera, regardless of its orientation.

m.d:
Determines to what degree the colors of the beam are blended with the colors behind it. It should be set in the range of 0 to 1. A value of 0 uses normal blending modes and a value of 1 uses additive blending.

This property should not be confused with LightInfluence which determines how the beam is affected by environmental light.

This property does not cause the beam to light the environment.
m.s: Determines to what degree the colors of the beam are blended with the colors behind it.

m.d:
Determines the degree to which the beam is influenced by the environment's lighting, clamped between 0 and 1. When 0, the beam will be unaffected by the environment's lighting. When 1, it will be fully affected by lighting as a BasePart would be.

See also LightEmission which specifies to what degree the colors of the beam are blended with the colors behind it.
m.s: Determines the degree to which the beam is influenced by the environment's lighting.

m.d:
The LocalTransparencyModifier property is a multiplier applied to the beam's Transparency that is only visible to the local client. It does not replicate from client to server and is useful for when a beam should not render for a specific client.

Uses the same formula as BasePart.LocalTransparencyModifier.

A value of 0 (default) has no effect on the beam's transparency. A value of 1 makes the beam completely invisible to the local client regardless of its Transparency value.
m.s: Determines a multiplier for `Class.Beam.Transparency` that is only visible to the local client.

m.d:
Rather than being a perfect curve, a beam is made up of straight segments. The more segments, the higher the resolution of the curve. The Segments property sets how many straight segments the beam is made up of, with a default value of 10.

Note that the Color and Transparency properties require a certain number of segments to display correctly. This is because each segment can only show a transition between two colors or transparencies. Therefore a Beam requires at least n-1 segments to display correctly, where n is the number of keypoint associated with the beam's Color and Transparency.
m.s: Sets how many straight segments the beam is made up of.

m.d:
The content ID of the texture to be displayed on the beam. If this property is not set, the beam will be displayed as a solid line; this also occurs when the texture is set to an invalid content ID or the image associated with the texture has not yet loaded.

The appearance of the texture can be further modified by other beam properties including Color and Transparency.

Scaling of the texture is determined by the TextureMode, TextureLength, Width0, and Width1 properties.
m.s: The content ID of the texture to be displayed on the beam.

m.d:
The texture displayed on the beam. Supports asset URIs.

If this property is set to Content.none, the beam displays as a solid line colored by its Color property. The appearance of the texture can be further modified by Color, Transparency, and scaling is determined by TextureMode, TextureLength, Width0, and Width1.
m.s: The texture displayed on the beam. Supports [asset URIs](../../../projects/assets/index.md#asset-uris).

m.d: Sets the length of the beam's texture, dependent on TextureMode.
m.s: Sets the length of the beam's texture, dependent on `Class.Beam.TextureMode|TextureMode`.

m.d:
This property, alongside TextureLength, determines how a beam's Texture repeats.

When set to TextureMode.Wrap or TextureMode.Static, the texture repetitions will equal the beam's overall length (in studs) divided by its TextureLength.

When set to TextureMode.Stretch, the texture will repeat TextureLength times across the beam's overall length.
m.s: Determines the manner in which the `Class.Beam.Texture|Texture` scales and repeats.

m.d:
Sets the number of texture cycles per second at which the Texture image moves along the beam, where one cycle is a full traversal of the texture's UV range. When this property is a positive value, the beam's texture will move from Attachment0 to Attachment1. This direction can be inverted by setting this property to a negative number. The default value is 1.

How far one cycle travels along the beam in studs depends on TextureMode and TextureLength.

Examples

  • -2 — Texture scrolls from Attachment1 toward Attachment0, completing two cycles per second.
  • 0 — Texture is static.
  • 1 — Texture scrolls from Attachment0 toward Attachment1, completing one cycle per second (default).
  • 2 — Texture scrolls from Attachment0 toward Attachment1, completing two cycles per second.
m.s: Determines the speed at which the `Class.Beam.Texture|Texture` image moves along the beam.

m.d:
Determines the transparency of the beam across its segments. This property is a NumberSequence, allowing the transparency to be configured to vary across the length of the beam.

Consider the following NumberSequence which, when applied to a beam, would yield the pictured result.

local numberSequence = NumberSequence.new({
        NumberSequenceKeypoint.new(0, 0), -- Opaque
        NumberSequenceKeypoint.new(0.5, 1), -- Transparent
        NumberSequenceKeypoint.new(1, 0), -- Opaque
    }
)

Note that the beam's transparency also depends on the number of Segments. Each segment of the beam can only show a transition between two transparencies. Therefore a beam will need to have at least n-1 segments in order to display correctly, where n is the number of NumberSequenceKeypoints in the NumberSequence.
m.s: Determines the transparency of the beam across its segments.

m.d: The width of the beam at its origin (Attachment0), in studs. The beam's width will change linearly to Width1 studs at its end (Attachment1).
m.s: The width of the beam at its origin (`Class.Beam.Attachment0|Attachment0`), in studs.

m.d: The width of the beam at its end (Attachment1), in studs. The beam's width will change linearly from Width0 studs at its origin (Attachment0).
m.s: The width of the beam at its end (`Class.Beam.Attachment1|Attachment1`), in studs.

m.d:
The distance, in studs, the beam display is offset relative to the CurrentCamera. When 0, the beam will be displayed in its standard position between Attachment0 and Attachment1. ZOffset can be either positive or negative.

This property is particularly useful to avoid "Z‑fighting" when using multiple Beams between the same Attachments.
m.s: The distance, in studs, the beam display is offset relative to the `Class.Workspace.CurrentCamera|CurrentCamera`.

m.d:
The offset of a beam's texture cycle represents the progress of its texture animation. This method sets the current offset of the beam's texture cycle; hence, it can be used to reset the cycle by passing 0 as the offset parameter.

Notes

  • The given offset parameter is expected to be a value between 0 and 1, but greater values can be used.
  • The texture cycle wraps at 0 and 1, meaning the texture is in the same position when the offset is at 0 or 1.
  • If the Texture property is not set, this method does nothing.
  • Increasing the offset will act in the inverse direction to the TextureSpeed property, meaning it will move the texture in the opposite direction to the direction the texture animates when TextureSpeed is greater than 0.
m.s: Sets the current offset of the beam's texture cycle.

p.s: The desired offset of the texture cycle.

class/BillboardGui.d:
BillboardGui is a container for UI objects to appear in the 3D space but always face the camera. The container's position is relative to the parent BasePart or Attachment (or the Adornee). For BaseParts, the Position property is used, while for Attachments, the WorldPosition property is used.

A billboard's Size property works slightly differently than GuiObject.Size. While the offset components work the same, the scale components are used as stud sizes in 3D space.

When creating a size-scaled BillboardGui that contains a TextLabel, it's useful to enable the label's TextScaled property so that its text scales along with the billboard canvas as the camera distance changes.

Note that interactive UI elements like ImageButtons and TextButtons inside a BillboardGui will only receive user input if they are parented to the PlayerGui, typically via placing the BillboardGui inside StarterGui. The Adornee property can be used to target a part or attachment in the 3D world while the BillboardGui itself remains in the PlayerGui.

See In-Experience UI for a guide on working with BillboardGui containers.

Caching Behavior

To help improve performance, the appearance of a BillboardGui is cached until one of the following occurs, after which its appearance will be recomputed on the next rendering frame.

  • A descendant is added to or removed from the BillboardGui.
  • A property of a descendant of the BillboardGui changes.
  • A property of the BillboardGui itself changes.
class/BillboardGui.s: A container for `Class.GuiObject|GuiObjects` that renders in 3D space facing the camera.

m.d:
Controls whether the descendants will receive input events. If the BillboardGui contains a GuiButton, that button will become clickable only if Active is set to true on both the BillboardGui and the button.

Note that interactive UI elements like ImageButtons and TextButtons inside a BillboardGui will only receive user input if they are parented to the PlayerGui, typically via placing the BillboardGui inside StarterGui. The Adornee property can be used to target a part or attachment in the 3D world while the BillboardGui itself remains in the PlayerGui.
m.s: Controls whether the descendants will receive input events.

kid.simple: Whether buttons inside can be clicked. A button in a BillboardGui is clickable only when Active is true on BOTH the BillboardGui and the button, and the BillboardGui is in the player's PlayerGui.
kid.example:
local billboard = script.Parent -- a BillboardGui in StarterGui with Adornee set
billboard.Active = true

m.d: Sets the target BasePart or Attachment that the BillboardGui is positioned relative to, overriding the parent part or attachment.
m.s: Sets the target part or attachment that the `Class.BillboardGui` is positioned relative to.

kid.simple: The part or attachment the billboard floats at. Setting it overrides the parent, so the BillboardGui can live in StarterGui (needed for clickable buttons) while still showing over a part in the world.
kid.example:
-- LocalScript; a BillboardGui named "Marker" is in StarterGui
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local playerGui = Players.LocalPlayer:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")
local marker = playerGui:WaitForChild("Marker")
marker.Adornee = workspace:WaitForChild("QuestGiver")

m.d:
This property determines whether the BillboardGui will always render on top of other 3D objects.

When set to false (default), the BillboardGui renders like other 3D content and is occluded by other 3D objects. When set to true, the BillboardGui always renders on top of 3D content and the appearance changes significantly:

  • Colors match how they appear inside a ScreenGui.
  • Text may appear sharper on high DPI devices.
  • LightInfluence is treated as though it's 0.
  • Brightness has no effect.
m.s: Determines whether the `Class.BillboardGui` will always be rendered on top of other 3D objects.

kid.simple: When true, the billboard is drawn on top of everything, so walls and parts can't hide it. Colors then look like normal screen UI and lighting is ignored. When false (default), it can be hidden behind things like a real object.
kid.example:
local billboard = script.Parent
billboard.AlwaysOnTop = true -- see it through walls

m.d:
This property determines the factor by which the BillboardGui container's light is scaled when LightInfluence is 0. By default, this property is 1 and can be set to any number between 0 and 1000. By modifying this property, the apparent brightness of a BillboardGui can be better matched to its environment. For instance, a video billboard can be brightened inside a dark room by increasing Brightness to 10.

Note that Brightness is inaccessible in Studio and has no effect when either LightInfluence is 1 or AlwaysOnTop is true.
m.s: Determines the factor by which the `Class.BillboardGui` container's light is scaled when `Class.BillboardGui.LightInfluence|LightInfluence` is `0`.

kid.simple: How bright the billboard glows when LightInfluence is 0. Default is 1, can go up to 1000. Turn it up to make a screen in a dark room pop.
kid.example:
local billboard = script.Parent
billboard.LightInfluence = 0
billboard.Brightness = 5
kid.gotcha: Does nothing if LightInfluence is 1 or AlwaysOnTop is true.

m.d:
When set to true (default), portions of GuiObjects that fall outside of the BillboardGui canvas borders will not be drawn.

Even when this property is false, GuiObjects that are completely outside of the canvas will not render.
m.s: Whether portions of `Class.GuiObject|GuiObjects` that fall outside of the `Class.BillboardGui` canvas borders will be drawn.

kid.simple: When true (default), parts of UI inside that stick out past the billboard's edges are cut off. UI completely outside the billboard is never drawn, even when false.
kid.example:
local billboard = script.Parent
billboard.ClipsDescendants = false

m.d: The current distance in studs that the BillboardGui is from the player's camera. A changed event does not fire for this property unless DistanceStep is more than 0.
m.s: The current distance in studs that the `Class.BillboardGui` is from the player's camera.

kid.simple: Read-only. How far away, in studs, the billboard is from the player's camera right now.
kid.example:
local billboard = script.Parent
print("Camera is", billboard.CurrentDistance, "studs away")
kid.gotcha: Its change event only fires if DistanceStep is more than 0.

m.d: Determines the distance in studs at which the BillboardGui will stop scaling larger in size relative to the player's current camera, with a default of 0. If the CurrentDistance of the BillboardGui is below this value, it will not scale any larger than it would at this distance.
m.s: Determines the distance in studs at which the `Class.BillboardGui` will stop scaling larger in size.
m.dep: Deprecated.

kid.simple: Old — use MaxDistance and a Size using Scale or Offset instead.

m.d: Determines the size CurrentDistance increments and decrements in studs as the player's camera moves closer and further from the BillboardGui. The property defaults to 0.
m.s: Determines the size `Class.BillboardGui.CurrentDistance|CurrentDistance` increments and decrements in studs as the player's camera moves closer and further from the `Class.BillboardGui`.

kid.simple: How many studs the camera must move before CurrentDistance updates. Default 0. Set it above 0 if you want to listen for CurrentDistance changes.
kid.example:
local billboard = script.Parent
billboard.DistanceStep = 5 -- update CurrentDistance every 5 studs
billboard:GetPropertyChangedSignal("CurrentDistance"):Connect(function()
	print("Now", billboard.CurrentDistance, "studs away")
end)

m.d:
Determines the distance in studs at which the BillboardGui will stop scaling smaller in size relative to the player's current camera. If the CurrentDistance of the BillboardGui is above this value, it will not scale any smaller than it would at this distance.

This property is ignored if the value is less than 0. The default value is -1, meaning the property is ignored by default.
m.s: Determines the distance in studs at which the `Class.BillboardGui` will stop scaling smaller in size.
m.dep: Deprecated.

kid.simple: Old — use MaxDistance and a Size using Scale or Offset instead.

m.d:
This property determines how the BillboardGui is offset from its Adornee, relative to the Camera orientation, in units half the dimensions of the model's Camera-aligned bounding box.

See also StudsOffset which works similarly but uses stud units, or ExtentsOffsetWorldSpace which works similarly except the offset orientation is relative to the global axes.
m.s: Determines how the `Class.BillboardGui` is offset from its `Class.BillboardGui.Adornee|Adornee`, relative to the `Class.Camera` orientation, in units half the dimensions of the model's `Class.Camera`-aligned bounding box.

kid.simple: Shifts the billboard away from its part, measured in 'half the part's size' units, along the camera's directions (right, up, toward camera). For a part 4 studs tall, ExtentsOffset (0, 1, 0) moves the billboard up 2 studs, right to the top edge.
kid.example:
local billboard = script.Parent
billboard.ExtentsOffset = Vector3.new(0, 1, 0) -- sit at the top edge of the part

m.d:
This property determines how the BillboardGui is offset from its Adornee, relative to the global axes, in units half the dimensions of the model's axis-aligned bounding box.

See also StudsOffset which works similarly but uses stud units, or ExtentsOffset which works similarly except the offset orientation is relative to the Camera.
m.s: Determines how the `Class.BillboardGui` is offset from its `Class.BillboardGui.Adornee|Adornee`, relative to the global axes, in units half the dimensions of the model's axis-aligned bounding box.

kid.simple: Like ExtentsOffset (shift in 'half the part's size' units), but the directions are the world's fixed X, Y, Z instead of the camera's.
kid.example:
local billboard = script.Parent
billboard.ExtentsOffsetWorldSpace = Vector3.new(0, 1, 0) -- always world 'up'

m.d: Controls how much the BillboardGui is influenced by environmental lighting, in a range from 0 to 1. Setting this to 1 means that surrounding lighting has complete control over the appearance, while setting it to 0 means that the lighting has no effect.
m.s: Controls how much the `Class.BillboardGui` is influenced by environmental lighting.

kid.simple: How much the world's lighting affects the billboard, from 0 to 1. 1 = fully affected (dark at night), 0 = not affected at all (always bright).
kid.example:
local billboard = script.Parent
billboard.LightInfluence = 0 -- stays bright even at night

m.d:
This property controls how far from the camera the BillboardGui will be displayed before it stops rendering. A value of 0 or inf (default) means there is no limit and it will render infinitely far away.

For BillboardGuis that appear outdoors, it's recommended that MaxDistance is high enough to ensure that the container's UI is sufficiently small on the screen when it appears or disappears, minimizing the sudden pop‑in/out effect.
m.s: Controls how far away the `Class.BillboardGui` can be displayed before it stops rendering.

kid.simple: How far away (in studs) the camera can be before the billboard disappears. 0 or infinity (the default) means it never disappears.
kid.example:
local billboard = script.Parent
billboard.MaxDistance = 60 -- only show when the camera is within 60 studs

m.d:
Used by scripts to hide the BillboardGui from a specific player.

To hide a BillboardGui from more than one player, place it into StarterGui and use a script to set the Enabled property according to whether the LocalPlayer should be able to see it. The Adornee property can be used to attach the BillboardGui to a BasePart or Attachment in the Workspace, instead of parenting it.
m.s: Used by scripts to hide the `Class.BillboardGui` from a specific player.

kid.simple: One player who should NOT see this billboard. Great for hiding your own name tag from yourself while everyone else sees it.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService: name tag over each character, hidden from its owner
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
	player.CharacterAdded:Connect(function(character)
		local head = character:WaitForChild("Head")
		local tag = Instance.new("BillboardGui")
		tag.Size = UDim2.fromOffset(150, 40)
		tag.StudsOffset = Vector3.new(0, 2, 0)
		tag.PlayerToHideFrom = player -- the owner doesn't see their own tag
		tag.Parent = head
		local label = Instance.new("TextLabel")
		label.Size = UDim2.fromScale(1, 1)
		label.BackgroundTransparency = 1
		label.Text = player.DisplayName
		label.Parent = tag
	end)
end)
kid.gotcha: Only works for one player. To hide from many, put it in StarterGui and turn Enabled on or off per player in a LocalScript.

m.d: Controls the size that the BillboardGui will have on screen. Unlike GuiObject.Size, the scale components of this property set the billboard's stud size in 3D space.
m.s: Controls the size that the `Class.BillboardGui` will have on screen.

kid.simple: How big the billboard is. Special rule: the Scale numbers mean STUDS in the world (so it looks smaller when far away), and the Offset numbers mean screen PIXELS (so it stays the same size on screen). UDim2.fromScale(4, 1) = 4 studs by 1 stud. UDim2.fromOffset(200, 50) = 200 by 50 pixels at any distance.
kid.example:
local billboard = script.Parent
billboard.Size = UDim2.fromScale(6, 2)    -- a 6 x 2 stud sign in the world
-- or
billboard.Size = UDim2.fromOffset(200, 50) -- always 200 x 50 pixels on screen

m.d:
A 2D offset in size-relative units that acts like an anchor point. This can be used similarly to the GuiObject.AnchorPoint property, but the values are different.

Size Offset Explanation
0, 0 The default in which UI will be anchored at its center.
0.5, 0.5 UI will anchor at the bottom left.
0.5, -0.5 UI will anchor at the top left.
-0.5, 0.5 UI will anchor at the top right.
-0.5, -0.5 UI will anchor at the bottom right.

See also StudsOffset, StudsOffsetWorldSpace, ExtentsOffset, and ExtentsOffsetWorldSpace which are offset properties that work in 3D space instead.
m.s: A 2D offset in size-relative units that acts like an anchor point.

kid.simple: Slides the billboard around its spot, measured in fractions of its own size, a bit like AnchorPoint but with different numbers. (0, 0) default = centered on the spot. (0.5, 0.5) = the spot is at the bottom-left of the billboard. (-0.5, -0.5) = the spot is at the bottom-right.
kid.example:
local billboard = script.Parent
billboard.SizeOffset = Vector2.new(0, 0.5) -- billboard sits above the spot instead of centered on it

m.d:
This property determines how the BillboardGui is offset from its Adornee in studs, relative to the Camera orientation.

See also StudsOffsetWorldSpace which works similarly except the offset orientation is relative to the global axes.
m.s: Determines how the `Class.BillboardGui` is offset from its `Class.BillboardGui.Adornee|Adornee` in studs, relative to the `Class.Camera` orientation.

kid.simple: Moves the billboard away from its part by a number of studs, using the camera's directions: X = camera's right, Y = camera's up, Z = toward the camera. Vector3.new(0, 3, 0) floats it 3 studs above the part's center.
kid.example:
local billboard = script.Parent
billboard.StudsOffset = Vector3.new(0, 3, 0) -- 3 studs up

m.d:
This property determines how the BillboardGui is offset from its Adornee in studs, relative to the global axes.

See also StudsOffset which works similarly except the offset orientation is relative to the Camera.
m.s: Determines how the `Class.BillboardGui` is offset from its `Class.BillboardGui.Adornee|Adornee` in studs, relative to the global axes.

kid.simple: Moves the billboard away from its part by a number of studs along the world's fixed X, Y, Z directions (not the camera's). A part at (0, 5, 0) with StudsOffsetWorldSpace (2, 0, 0) puts the billboard at (2, 5, 0).
kid.example:
local billboard = script.Parent
billboard.StudsOffsetWorldSpace = Vector3.new(0, 4, 0) -- always 4 studs straight up

kid.simple: A BillboardGui shows UI floating in the 3D world that always turns to face your camera, like a name tag or health bar above a character's head. Put TextLabels and ImageLabels inside it and attach it to a part or an attachment. It stays at that spot in the world, but you always see it from the front.
kid.analogy: A BillboardGui is like a helium balloon with a picture on it, tied to a toy. Wherever the toy goes, the balloon follows, and it magically always turns its picture toward you.
whenToUse: Name tags or health bars above characters or enemies
Floating markers like an arrow or '!' over a quest giver
Price tags hovering above shop items
Damage numbers that pop up over something you hit
kid.where: Parent it to a Part or Attachment in Workspace (it floats at that part), or put it in StarterGui and set its Adornee to the part. Buttons inside only work if the BillboardGui is in the player's PlayerGui. Usually created or changed from a LocalScript, but a server Script can also put one in Workspace so everyone sees it.

terms.LocalScript: A script that runs on the player's own device. UI code goes in LocalScripts, because each player has their own copy of the UI.
terms.client: The player's own device: their computer, phone, tablet or console.
terms.server: Roblox's computer that runs the game for everyone at once.
terms.StarterGui: A folder in Explorer. UI you put here is copied to every player when they spawn.
terms.PlayerGui: Each player's own personal UI folder (inside their Player object). Only UI in here actually shows on their screen.
terms.descendant: Anything inside an object: children, grandchildren, and so on.
terms.3D world: The game world with parts and characters, as opposed to the flat screen UI.
terms.stud: Roblox's unit of distance. A default character is about 5 studs tall.
terms.Adornee: The part or attachment the BillboardGui is stuck to. It overrides the parent.
terms.Attachment: An invisible point inside a part that marks a spot, like the top of a head.
terms.offset: An extra shift from a starting point. StudsOffset (0, 3, 0) moves the billboard 3 studs up from the part's center.
terms.camera: Your eye in the game world: what decides what you see.
terms.occluded: Hidden behind something else, like a sign behind a wall.
terms.Scale (in BillboardGui Size): In a BillboardGui, the Scale part of Size means studs in the world, not a percent. Scale 4 = 4 studs wide.
terms.Offset (in BillboardGui Size): In a BillboardGui, the Offset part of Size is pixels on your screen, so it stays the same size no matter how far away you are.
terms.deprecated: Old and replaced by something better. Don't use it in new code.

examples.title: Put a name tag above a part
examples.place: Script in ServerScriptService (with a Part named "Shopkeeper" in Workspace)
examples.code:
local shopkeeper = workspace:WaitForChild("Shopkeeper")

local billboard = Instance.new("BillboardGui")
billboard.Size = UDim2.fromOffset(200, 50)  -- 200 x 50 pixels on screen, at any distance
billboard.StudsOffset = Vector3.new(0, 3, 0) -- float 3 studs above the part's center
billboard.AlwaysOnTop = true                  -- don't hide behind walls
billboard.MaxDistance = 100                   -- disappear when farther than 100 studs
billboard.Parent = shopkeeper                 -- attach to the part

local label = Instance.new("TextLabel")
label.Size = UDim2.fromScale(1, 1)            -- fill the whole billboard
label.BackgroundTransparency = 1              -- no box, just text
label.Text = "Shopkeeper"
label.TextColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(255, 255, 255)
label.TextStrokeTransparency = 0              -- black outline so it's easy to read
label.TextScaled = true
label.Parent = billboard
explain: Parenting the BillboardGui to the part makes it float at that part's position.
Size uses Offset (pixels), so the tag looks the same size on screen whether you're near or far.
StudsOffset (0, 3, 0) shifts it 3 studs up. If the part is at (10, 2, 5), the tag sits around (10, 5, 5).
Because this is a server Script and the billboard is in Workspace, every player sees it.

examples.title: A tag that shrinks with distance (world-sized)
examples.code:
local part = workspace:WaitForChild("Chest")

local billboard = Instance.new("BillboardGui")
billboard.Size = UDim2.fromScale(4, 1) -- 4 studs wide, 1 stud tall IN THE WORLD
billboard.StudsOffset = Vector3.new(0, 2, 0)
billboard.Parent = part

local label = Instance.new("TextLabel")
label.Size = UDim2.fromScale(1, 1)
label.BackgroundTransparency = 1
label.TextScaled = true -- text grows and shrinks with the billboard
label.Text = "Treasure!"
label.Parent = billboard
explain: In a BillboardGui, Size's Scale numbers mean studs. (4, 1) is a sign 4 studs wide and 1 stud tall.
Because it's world-sized, it looks smaller as you walk away, like a real sign.
TextScaled makes the text fit the sign at any distance.

gotchas: Size Scale works differently here: it means studs in the world, not a percent of the parent. Offset is still pixels.
Buttons inside a BillboardGui only get clicks if the BillboardGui is in PlayerGui (put it in StarterGui and set Adornee) AND Active is true on both the BillboardGui and the button.
If you can't see it, check that it has a parent part or an Adornee, and that it isn't hidden behind a wall (try AlwaysOnTop).
Offset-sized billboards stay big even far away, which can clutter the screen. Use MaxDistance to hide them.

class/BinaryStringValue.d: An internal type of StringValue object, that stores a BinaryString value.
class/BinaryStringValue.s: An internal type of `Class.StringValue` object, that stores a `BinaryString` value.

m.d:
Fires if the BinaryStringValue.Value of the BinaryStringValue is changed by the engine.

In practice, this object is stored out of reach from normal scripts, so this event cannot be connected to. If a BinaryStringValue is created by a script, the engine will not do anything with it, so the event will never fire.

Equivalent changed events exist for similar objects, such as NumberValue and StringValue, depending on what object type best suits the need.
m.s: Fires if the BinaryStringValue's value is changed.

p.s: The new value after the change.

class/BindableEvent.d:
The BindableEvent object enables custom events through asynchronous one-way communication between scripts on the same side of the client-server boundary. When you fire a BindableEvent through the BindableEvent:Fire() method, the firing script does not yield and the target function receives the passed arguments with certain limitations. BindableEvents create threads of each connected function, so even if one firing errors, others continue.

As an alternative for two-way communication between two scripts on the same side of the client-server boundary, consider BindableFunction.

As stated, BindableEvents do not allow for communication between the server and clients. If you are looking for this functionality, use a RemoteEvent as outlined in Remote Events and Callbacks.

See Bindable events and callbacks for code samples and further details on BindableEvent.

Parameter Limitations

Any type of Roblox object such as an Enum, Instance, or others can be passed as a parameter when a BindableEvent is fired, as well as Luau types such as numbers, strings, and booleans, although you should carefully explore the limitations.
class/BindableEvent.s: An object which enables custom events through asynchronous one-way communication between scripts on the same side of the client-server boundary. Scripts firing a `Class.BindableEvent` do not yield.

m.d:
Fires the BindableEvent which in turn fires the Event event. This method does not yield, even if no script has connected to the event, and even if a connected function yields.

Any type of Roblox object such as an Enum, Instance, or others can be passed as a parameter to Fire(), as well as Luau types such as numbers, strings, and booleans, although you should carefully explore the limitations.

See Bindable events and callbacks for code samples and further details on Fire().
m.s: Fires the `Class.BindableEvent` which in turn fires the `Class.BindableEvent.Event|Event` event.

p.s: Values to pass to Event events connected to the same BindableEvent.

kid.simple: Rings the bell. Every function connected to `.Event` runs, with the values you pass.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
local levelUp = Instance.new("BindableEvent")

levelUp.Event:Connect(function(newLevel)
	print("Reached level", newLevel)
end)

levelUp:Fire(5) --> Reached level 5

m.d:
Fires when any script calls the Fire() method on the same BindableEvent instance, using the same arguments as parameters.

See Bindable events and callbacks for code samples and further details on Event.
m.s: Fires when any script calls the `Class.BindableEvent:Fire()|Fire()` method on the same `Class.BindableEvent` instance.

p.s: The parameters sent through Fire().

kid.simple: The event that runs each time someone calls `Fire` on this BindableEvent. Connect a function to it to listen.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
local ServerStorage = game:GetService("ServerStorage")
local roundEnded = ServerStorage:WaitForChild("RoundEnded")

roundEnded.Event:Connect(function(winner)
	print("Winner:", winner)
end)

kid.simple: A BindableEvent lets scripts on the SAME side talk to each other: server Script to server Script, or LocalScript to LocalScript. One script fires it, and every script listening runs its function. It does not cross between server and players; that is what RemoteEvents are for.
kid.analogy: A BindableEvent is like a school bell inside one building. When someone rings it, every classroom in that building hears it. A building across the street (the other side of the client-server boundary) hears nothing.
whenToUse: One server Script needs to tell other server Scripts something happened, like 'round over'.
Making your own custom event, like a `Died` or `LevelUp` event for your own system.
Not for server-to-client messages. Use a RemoteEvent for that.
kid.where: Create it in Studio or with `Instance.new("BindableEvent")`. Put it where your scripts can find it, like ServerStorage (server-only) or ReplicatedStorage.

terms.server: The one computer, run by Roblox in a data center, that is in charge of a game. Every player in the same game is connected to it. It keeps the official copy of the game, like who has how many coins.
terms.client: Your own device (phone, PC, Xbox) running the game. Every player has their own client. The client draws the screen and reads your keyboard, mouse or touch.
terms.client-server boundary: The invisible wall between the server and each client. They are different computers, so a script on one side cannot just reach over and change a variable on the other side. Messages have to be sent across.
terms.fire: To send off an event so that the functions listening to it run.
terms.event / signal: Something that can happen, like `PlayerAdded` or `OnServerEvent`. You connect a function to it and that function runs each time it happens.
terms.connect: Telling Roblox: when this event happens, run my function. You do it with `:Connect(function() ... end)`.
terms.same side: Both scripts run on the server, or both run on the same player's client.

examples.title: Tell other server scripts the round ended
examples.place: Two Scripts in ServerScriptService, BindableEvent named RoundEnded in ServerStorage
examples.code:
-- Script A: the round timer
local ServerStorage = game:GetService("ServerStorage")
local roundEnded = ServerStorage:WaitForChild("RoundEnded")

task.wait(60)
roundEnded:Fire("Red team") -- tell everyone listening

-- Script B: gives out rewards
local ServerStorage = game:GetService("ServerStorage")
local roundEnded = ServerStorage:WaitForChild("RoundEnded")

roundEnded.Event:Connect(function(winner)
	print(winner .. " won! Giving rewards...")
end)
explain: Script A calls `Fire` with the winner's name.
Script B was listening with `.Event:Connect`, so its function runs and receives the same value.
Both scripts are on the server, so a BindableEvent is the right tool.

gotchas: It does not cross the client-server boundary. A LocalScript firing it will not reach a server Script.
Values are copied, not shared: if you fire a table, listeners get a copy, and functions or metatables inside it are lost.
Make sure the listener connects before you fire, or it will miss the message.

class/BindableFunction.d:
The BindableFunction object allows for synchronous two-way communication between scripts on the same side of the client-server boundary. You can use it to define a custom callback function and invoke it manually by calling BindableFunction:Invoke(). The code invoking the function yields until the corresponding callback is found, and the callback receives the arguments that you passed to Invoke(). If the callback was never set, the script that invokes it will not resume execution.

As an alternative for one-way communication between two scripts on the same side of the client-server boundary, consider BindableEvent which does not yield for a return.

As stated, BindableFunctions do not allow for communication between the server and clients. If you are looking for this functionality, use a RemoteFunction as outlined in Remote events and callbacks.

See Bindable events and callbacks for code samples and further details on BindableFunction.

Parameter Limitations

Any type of Roblox object such as an Enum, Instance, or others can be passed as a parameter when a BindableFunction is invoked, as well as Luau types such as numbers, strings, and booleans, although you should carefully explore the limitations.
class/BindableFunction.s: An object which allows for synchronous two-way communication between scripts on the same side of the client-server boundary. Scripts invoking a `Class.BindableFunction` yield until the corresponding callback is found.

m.d:
Invokes the BindableFunction which in turn calls the OnInvoke callback, returning any values returned by the callback. Invocations yield until the corresponding callback is found, and if the callback was never set, the script that invokes it will not resume execution.

Any type of Roblox object such as an Enum, Instance, or others can be passed as a parameter to Invoke(), as well as Luau types such as numbers, strings, and booleans, although you should carefully explore the limitations.

Only one function can be bound to Invoke() at a time. If you assign multiple functions, only the last one assigned will be used.

See Bindable events and callbacks for code samples and further details on Invoke().
m.s: Invokes the `Class.BindableFunction` which in turn calls the `Class.BindableFunction.OnInvoke|OnInvoke` callback, returning any values returned by the callback.

p.s: Values to pass to the OnInvoke callback.

r.s: Values returned from the OnInvoke callback.

kid.simple: Calls the function set in `OnInvoke` and waits for what it returns.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
local double = Instance.new("BindableFunction")
double.OnInvoke = function(n)
	return n * 2
end

print(double:Invoke(21)) --> 42

m.d:
This callback is called when the BindableFunction is invoked with Invoke(). It can be set multiple times but cannot be called directly. Invocations will yield until this callback is found and, if it is never set, the script that invoked it will not resume execution.

See Bindable events and callbacks for code samples and further details on OnInvoke.
m.s: Callback for when the `Class.BindableFunction` is invoked with `Class.BindableFunction:Invoke()|Invoke()`.

p.s: The parameters sent through Invoke().

r.s: Values returned by the callback function.

kid.simple: The function that answers when someone calls `Invoke`. Whatever it returns is sent back to the caller.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
local ServerStorage = game:GetService("ServerStorage")
local isVip = ServerStorage:WaitForChild("IsVip")

isVip.OnInvoke = function(player)
	return player:GetAttribute("VIP") == true
end

kid.simple: A BindableFunction lets one script ask another script on the SAME side a question and wait for the answer. It is like a RemoteFunction, but it does not travel between server and players.
kid.analogy: A BindableFunction is like asking a classmate in the same room 'what is the answer to number 3?' and waiting until they tell you. You cannot ask someone in a different building this way.
whenToUse: One server Script needs to get information from another server Script, like 'what level is this player?'.
Two LocalScripts on the same player need to share an answer.
Tip: a ModuleScript is often a simpler way to share functions between scripts.
kid.where: Create it in Studio or with `Instance.new("BindableFunction")`. The answering script sets `OnInvoke`; the asking script calls `Invoke`.

terms.server: The one computer, run by Roblox in a data center, that is in charge of a game. Every player in the same game is connected to it. It keeps the official copy of the game, like who has how many coins.
terms.client: Your own device (phone, PC, Xbox) running the game. Every player has their own client. The client draws the screen and reads your keyboard, mouse or touch.
terms.client-server boundary: The invisible wall between the server and each client. They are different computers, so a script on one side cannot just reach over and change a variable on the other side. Messages have to be sent across.
terms.invoke: To call a function and wait for its answer.
terms.callback: A function you give to Roblox to run later. You set `OnInvoke` with `=`.
terms.yield: To pause and wait. `Invoke` pauses your script until the answer comes back.
terms.ModuleScript: A script that holds shared code. Other scripts load it with `require`.

examples.title: Ask another script for a player's level
examples.place: Two Scripts in ServerScriptService, BindableFunction named GetLevel in ServerStorage
examples.code:
-- Script A: owns the level data
local ServerStorage = game:GetService("ServerStorage")
local getLevel = ServerStorage:WaitForChild("GetLevel")

local levels = {}

getLevel.OnInvoke = function(player)
	return levels[player.UserId] or 1
end

-- Script B: wants to know
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local ServerStorage = game:GetService("ServerStorage")
local getLevel = ServerStorage:WaitForChild("GetLevel")

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
	local level = getLevel:Invoke(player) -- waits for Script A
	print(player.Name .. " is level " .. level)
end)
explain: Script A sets `OnInvoke`, the function that answers.
Script B calls `Invoke(player)` and waits for the number Script A returns.

gotchas: Set `OnInvoke` with `=`. Only one answering function can exist; setting it again replaces it.
If nobody has set `OnInvoke` yet, `Invoke` waits until someone does.
Does not cross between server and client. Use a RemoteFunction for that.

class/BlockMesh.d:
The BlockMesh object applies a 'brick' mesh to the BasePart it is parented to. It behaves identically to a SpecialMesh with SpecialMesh.MeshType set to 'brick'.

What does a BlockMesh do?

A BlockMesh gives the BasePart it was applied to a brick shaped mesh. It is identical in appearance to a standard Roblox Part.

The dimensions of the mesh will scale linearly in all directions with BasePart.Size, this means a part containing a BlockMesh can be resized the same way as any other part.

The additional functionality a BlockMesh brings however, is the ability to set the DataModelMesh.Scale and DataModelMesh.Offset properties. These allow the position and dimensions of the mesh that is displayed to be changed without changing the BasePart.Position or BasePart.Size of the BasePart the mesh is parented to.

Note as the BlockMesh object does not include a texture the DataModelMesh.VertexColor property does not do anything.
class/BlockMesh.s: The BlockMesh object applies a 'brick' mesh to the `Class.BasePart` it is parented to. It behaves identically to a `Class.SpecialMesh` with `Class.SpecialMesh.MeshType` set to 'Brick'.

class/BodyForce.d:
The BodyForce object applies (or exerts) a force on the assembly to which it is parented. If the magnitude of such a force is great enough, assemblies can begin to accelerate. The force is determined by the Force property, and is defined on the three world axes.

A BodyForce alone cannot apply a torque (it cannot cause the parent to rotate on its own). To apply a force at a specific point or apply forces relative to the orientation of the assembly, use a BodyThrust instead.
class/BodyForce.s: Applies a constant force to an object.
class/BodyForce.dep: This object is deprecated and should not be used for new work. Use VectorForce instead, and see the legacy conversion notes.

m.d: This property determines the magnitude of force exerted on each axis, relative to the world.
m.s: Determines the force exerted on each axis.

m.s: Determines the amount of force applied on each axis.
m.dep: This deprecated property is a variant of BodyForce.Force which should be used instead.

class/BodyGyro.d:
The BodyGyro object applies a torque (rotational force) on an assembly such that it maintains a constant angular displacement, or orientation. This allows for the creation of assemblies that point in a certain direction, as if a real gyroscope were acting upon it. Essentially, it's the rotational counterpart to a BodyPosition.

If you would like to maintain a constant angular velocity, use a BodyAngularVelocity instead.

The CFrame property controls the goal orientation. Only the angular components of the CFrame are used; position will make no difference. MaxTorque limits the amount of angular force that may be applied, P controls the power used in achieving the goal orientation, and D controls dampening behavior.
class/BodyGyro.s: Applies a torque to maintain a constant orientation.
class/BodyGyro.dep: This object is deprecated and should not be used for new work. Use AlignOrientation instead, and see the legacy conversion notes.

m.d: This property (not to be confused with BasePart.CFrame) determines the target orientation towards which torque will be exerted. Since BodyGyro does not apply translational force, the translational/positional component of the CFrame is ignored. Consider using one of the following CFrame constructors in setting this property: CFrame.fromAxisAngle(), CFrame.fromEulerAnglesXYZ(), or CFrame.fromEulerAnglesYXZ().
m.s: Determines the target orientation (translational component ignored).

m.dep: This property is a deprecated variant of BodyGyro.CFrame which should be used instead.

m.d: This property defines how much dampening will be applied to the torque used to reach the goal CFrame. When the assembly approaches the goal orientation, it needs to decelerate, otherwise it will rotate past the goal and have to stop and re-accelerate back toward the goal. This often creates an undesirable "rubber‑banding" effect, avoided by applying dampening. The higher this value is set, the greater the dampening curve becomes, or the slower the assembly will approach the goal orientation.
m.s: Determines the amount of dampening to use in reaching the goal `Class.BodyGyro.CFrame|CFrame`.

m.d: This property determines the limit on the amount of torque that may be applied on each axis in reaching the goal orientation (CFrame). If an assembly isn't moving, consider increasing this value and also check that it is not Anchored or attached to any anchored assemblies.
m.s: Determines the limit on how much torque that may be applied to each axis.

m.dep: This property is a deprecated variant of BodyGyro.MaxTorque which should be used instead.

m.d: This property determines how much power is used while applying torque in order to reach the goal CFrame. The higher this value, the more power will be used and the faster it will be used.
m.s: Determines how aggressive of a torque is applied in reaching the goal orientation.

class/BodyMover.d:
BodyMover is the abstract base class for the set of legacy objects that exert forces to assemblies in different ways. In general, the subclasses of BodyMover are:

  • BodyForce exerts a force relative to world coordinates.
  • BodyPosition exerts force to maintain a certain world position.
  • BodyVelocity exerts force to maintain a certain velocity.
  • BodyThrust exerts a force relative to object coordinates which applies torque if positioned in a certain way.
  • BodyGyro exerts torque to maintain a certain orientation.
  • BodyAngularVelocity exerts torque to maintain a certain angular velocity.
  • RocketPropulsion exerts both translational and rotational forces to cause an assembly to track down another.
class/BodyMover.s: Base class for objects that continually exert forces to assemblies.
class/BodyMover.dep: This class has been deprecated. See the mover constraints article for an overview of BodyMover replacements, as well as the legacy conversion notes.

class/BodyPosition.d:
The BodyPosition object applies a force on an assembly such that it will maintain a constant position in the world. The Position property, not to be confused with BasePart.Position, controls the target world position. This is the translational counterpart to a BodyGyro.

If you need further control on a force applied to an object, consider using a BodyForce or BodyThrust instead.

The strength of the force applied by this object is controlled by several factors, namely the distance to the goal position: the force is stronger when farther away from the goal. This is amplified by P (power). The present velocity will also dampen the force applied by this object, and this is amplified by D (dampening). The resulting force is then capped by MaxForce. Note the force applied on the assembly to achieve the goal position may vary on a per-axis basis.

When the assembly approaches the goal position it needs to decelerate, otherwise it will move past the goal and have to stop and re-accelerate back toward the goal. This is often creates an undesirable "rubber‑banding" effect, avoided by applying dampening. The higher this value is set, the greater the dampening curve becomes, or the slower the assembly will approach the goal position.

The force the BodyPosition exerts increases as the difference between the assembly's current position and the goal position increases. This property is multiplied to this force to either amplify or diminish it.

class/Bone.d:
Bones are non-rendered objects that drive the movement of one or more parts for the purposes of animation, or creating clothing and characters. Bones are part of a Model or MeshPart object's skeletal rig that you typically access and animate through the Animation Editor.

Rigs are created during the modeling process in third-party software such as Blender or Maya. After importing the rigged model into Studio, you can add the model directly to your experience, or save and share the model as an asset. See Rigging for more details on creating and using rigged models.

Note that you can parent Bones under other Bones and parts. When parenting a bone to another bone, the child bone's world position will be relative to the parent bone's position, and the hierarchy of parented Bone objects can change the behavior of affected parts during posing or animation.

Relationship with Motor6D

To support animations with older rigs using joints, such as Motor6D, you can use the Bone.Transform property in the same way as Motor6D.Transform. Roblox uses the offset of the bones from the default pose to drive an animation, and bones are not replicated or serialized.

Bone.CFrame

Bones inherit the CFrame property of Attachments which Roblox uses as the bone's reference position. The inherited WorldCFrame and other world properties return the initial un-transformed position.
class/Bone.s: Bones are non-rendered objects that drive the movement of one or more parts for the purposes of animation, or creating clothing and characters.

Transform determines the current animated offset of the bone relative to its CFrame. This property is set by Roblox when animations on skinned meshes are played, although it can be manipulated manually in a manner similar to Motor6D.Transform.

  • TransformedCFrame and TransformedWorldCFrame, whose values are partially determined by this property

class/BrowserService.d:
This service is reserved for Roblox's own code and isn't accessible from experience scripts.

BrowserService bridges the Roblox client to its native web browser or embedded WebView. It opens browser windows and native overlays, runs JavaScript inside the resulting WebView, and relays messages to and from the web-side hybrid bridge (window.Roblox.Hybrid).

OpenBrowserWindow opens a URL only if it is allowlisted (a Roblox site, a youtube.com/watch page, or a stripe.com or vnggames.com subdomain); otherwise the request is rejected. OpenNativeOverlay opens a native overlay for Roblox URLs only. SendCommand forwards a JSON command to the WebView, ExecuteJavaScript evaluates a script inside it, and CloseBrowserWindow closes it. OpenWeChatAuthWindow launches the Tencent (WeChat) authentication flow, while ReturnToJavaScript and EmitHybridEvent invoke callbacks and dispatch events on the web-side hybrid bridge. Signals such as BrowserWindowClosed, BrowserWindowWillNavigate, JavaScriptCallback, and AuthCookieCopiedToEngine report WebView activity back to the client.
class/BrowserService.s: Bridges the Roblox client to its native web browser or WebView.
